text:
BIDDEFORD — The first city council meeting since Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero was shot and killed by a federal immigration agent began last week as all municipal meetings do: with the Pledge of Allegiance.

“With liberty and justice for all.”

The six words hung over the crowd of some 75 people gathered in the high school auditorium.

Over the next two hours, dozens of residents stepped up to the microphone. They shared their grief. They shared their anger. They shared a sense that leaders in Biddeford and across Maine aren’t doing enough to prevent another tragedy at the hands of Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

But confronted with federal officers from an opaque agency shattering car windows and violently confronting neighbors, those in the crowd and many of the officials they’re demanding results from are stuck with a difficult dilemma: What power do local officials have over federal agents seemingly acting with a sense of impunity?

What justice will come for Guerrero?

Advertisement

“It’s sad that it’s come to this point. Saying that there’s not much that we can do, that just isn’t enough. It’s just not,” said Biddeford resident Evan Lockwood. “There has to be something.”

“If there’s nothing that (city councilors) can do, then what’s the point of all this?” asked business owner Kelsey Cummings. “Why are we here?”

“Our communities today are actively under attack,” said Tophe Thorne, an immigrant advocate with Presente! Maine. “We are asking this council to stand with us with actions and not statements.”

The community’s outrage was palpable in the hours immediately after the shooting. Hundreds of residents protested, swarming the streets and shutting down Biddeford’s downtown. They were animated, initiating a brief standoff with police after marching into Sen. Susan Collins’ office on Main Street over her vote earlier this year to increase ICE funding.

But as the days wore on, that outrage turned to grief. The crowd of protestors holding signs at Mechanics Park dwindled. The number of flowers and candles at the intersection where Guerrero was shot grew. His blood stain remained on the asphalt.

Where community members were looking for an outlet in the aftermath of the shooting, they’re now looking for answers. Guerrero’s killing and residents’ pleas for action in its wake have prompted wider questions about the power — if any — local authorities have over federal offices and their agents.

Advertisement

The local officials they’re asking don’t have the answers yet. They aren’t sure they ever will.

“There’s this sort of sense of grief and sadness. We’re trying to fight that feeling of hopelessness with action,” said Biddeford city councilor Abigail Woods, who lives just a block away from where Guerrero was shot.

“But what can we actually do about this?”

UNANSWERABLE QUESTIONS REMAIN

The questions Biddeford residents are asking — about what prompted ICE to shoot Guerrero in the street, whether the federal investigation into the incident will be fair and transparent, and whether David Brouillette, the agent who shot Guerrero, will be held accountable — are the same questions that a growing number of cities across the country have asked their leaders.

There have been at least 30 instances across the country of federal immigration agents firing on civilians in cars since President Donald Trump began an immigration crackdown during his second term, according to NPR. At least seven of those incidents were deadly.

In March last year, U.S. citizen Ruben Ray Martinez was shot and killed by an ICE agent while behind the wheel in Texas. In January, Renée Good was gunned down in the front seat of her car in a suburb of Minneapolis. And just days before Guerrero’s death, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was similarly shot dead in his car by an immigration officer in Houston.

Advertisement

In each of those cities, answers from local leaders and ICE officials have been hard to come by.

The agency said it has investigated its officers in the wake of each shooting. But ICE has stymied some local investigations and largely kept the results of its own reviews, including whether the agents involved faced any disciplinary action, under seal.

ICE spokespeople have not responded to the Press Herald’s repeated requests for comment on the status of the investigation into Guerrero’s death. Nor have they answered questions about the precise chain of events that ended with agents handcuffing Guerrero’s limp body as he lay bleeding on the ground with a gunshot wound to his head.

SILENCE AMONG LAW ENFORCEMENT

ICE’s cooperation with other agencies, both federal and local, has shifted drastically under the second Trump administration.

Historically, outside federal agencies have investigated alongside local authorities when a federal agent has used deadly force, said Katherine Hawkins, a senior legal analyst with the nonprofit watchdog organization Project on Government Oversight. Those investigations often resulted in disciplinary action or criminal charges.

But that collaboration and admittedly thin sense of accountability has largely evaporated over the last two years, Hawkins said.

Advertisement

The FBI, which has historically investigated federal use of force incidents, has reportedly been told to stand down on ICE investigations. The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, will now investigate itself, NBC News reported.

After two American citizens were killed by ICE agents in Minnesota in January, federal officials portrayed them as domestic terrorists trying to attack immigration officers. When local law enforcement began investigating the shootings, they said the Department of Homeland Security withheld key evidence until this month.

“What happened in Minnesota, it was an agency that wasn’t even going through the motions of a professional investigation in the early days,” Hawkins said. “The officers weren’t even put on administrative leave.”

This month, Trump suddenly and publicly reversed a decision to end all ICE traffic stops instituted in the wake of the shootings in Biddeford and Texas. The Intercept reported this week that ICE has tightened its uniform requirements to mandate agents be publicly identifiable, though they are still allowed to wear face masks.

Vice President JD Vance has asserted that federal agents have “absolute immunity,” even when it comes to the use of deadly force.

While federal agents do have qualified immunity for some of their actions, Hawkins said they are not exempt from state and local laws. There have been instances, even in recent months, of ICE agents being charged for physical and sexual abuse, among other crimes.

Advertisement

Though Brouillette is reportedly being held in protective government custody, it remains unclear whether he will face any repercussions or criminal charges for Guerrero’s death.

Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey’s office is investigating the shooting, as it does all law enforcement killings in the state. To this point, the office says federal authorities have cooperated with state investigators’ efforts.

The AG’s office has never found an officer-involved shooting in Maine to be unjustified.

A spokesperson for Frey’s office said Thursday they “continue to work cooperatively with our federal partners” but declined to answer questions about the status of the investigation, the extent to which federal authorities are assisting or a rough time frame for when the investigation will be complete.

But when it comes to standard immigration enforcement, ICE has maintained radio silence with Maine officials at all levels, complicating many local departments’ work and conflicting with some leaders’ basic understanding of probable cause.

Biddeford’s police Chief JoAnne Fisk did not respond to requests for comment on this story. York County Sheriff Bill King said ICE has never had any contact with his office or its deputies about their operations, even before Maine legislators moved to enact a law prohibiting local police from collaborating with ICE.

Advertisement

The York County Jail, as with many in Maine, has several immigrants on its staff. Many of them have been on edge since ICE’s arrest of a Cumberland County corrections officer in January, King said. They and many others in southern Maine’s immigrant communities have watched as ICE conducted raids and made arrests without any warning or explanation.

And on the other end of law enforcement, when King’s deputies make a targeted arrest, “We know who they are,” he said. His office has conducted pre-surveillance and built enough evidence not just to prosecute, but to know they have the correct target. When federal agencies like the FBI or DEA do the same in the course of their own investigations, they generally let local sheriffs and police know, almost as a courtesy.

ICE on the other hand, King noted, said Guerrero wasn’t the subject of the warrant agents were serving that clear Monday morning he was killed. The agency hasn’t provided clarification about who they were targeting or why. And for the last year, their actions in Biddeford, York County and the rest of Maine have been carried out largely in the shadows.

“It all begs the question, to me: Do they even have a plan? Is this all haphazard?” King asked. “I’m sure some of the guys (ICE) is looking for are bad guys. But does it call for this? For putting the public in danger?”

“And then they want to investigate themselves?”

THE CITY AND THE FEDS

Residents at the Biddeford council meeting last week asked police to prevent ICE from coming into town or monitoring their activity in the city. Several invoked a 1924 Ku Klux Klan march from Saco to Biddeford that was broken up on the Main Street Bridge by then-Mayor Edward Drapeau and a crowd of Irish- and Franco-Americans.

Advertisement

“We need leaders that say like Mayor Drapeau did 100 years ago, ‘We’re drawing the line at the bridge,'” resident Jonathan Haines said at last week’s meeting. “Dirigo. I lead. Let Biddeford, let Maine, be the one that stops (them) at the bridge.”

It’s unlikely local officials could actually do that, though.

The municipal government and local law enforcement ultimately have little authority over ICE and its agents’ activity, Biddeford Mayor Liam LaFountain said. The federal government supersedes most any authority local governments may try to exert. The city can change its ordinances, the state can investigate the shooting, but ICE’s policies and protocols are at their own discretion.

There have been discussions about drafting a policy to prevent municipal employees from interacting with ICE, LaFountain said, similar to an ordinance Waterville adopted last week. But that would largely be codifying what’s already the city’s standard practice, he said.

“This is a federal agency that we’re dealing with. With federal resources approved by Congress,” LaFountain said. “To rein them in, that’s not something an individual city government can do, even if the majority view of the people who live here want us to.”

“It’s uncharted territory.”

Advertisement

Others are worried rebuking ICE could incur federal retaliation.

King, the county sheriff, recalled when Cumberland County Sheriff Kevin Joyce called ICE’s January arrest of a corrections officer in his car “bush league.” The agency abruptly pulled all of its detainees — and a sizable chunk of federal funding — from the Cumberland County Jail days later and publicly chastised Joyce for employing an “illegal alien.”

“How are we gonna fight the feds?” King said. “Look at the price Kevin paid.”

IT TAKES A VILLAGE

Ultimately, it seems any changes to how ICE conducts itself will likely be prompted by public outcry.

LaFountain, Woods and other municipal officials are reckoning with the small amount of leeway they have over the agency. King and Fisk, the police chief, are fielding calls for action they know they can’t heed. The only people with authority to affect how ICE enforces immigration law are in Congress and the executive branch of the federal government.

Still, public backlash has already affected how the Trump administration is deploying ICE, Hawkins noted. Greg Bovino, the former chief of Customs and Border Patrol, and former Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem were both ousted amid uproars over their agencies’ enforcement tactics and responses to the killings of American citizens in Minnesota and elsewhere.

Advertisement

“Outcry at both the local and national level does have some effect on the calculations authorities make,” Hawkins said. “It makes a major difference whether local law enforcement is actively cooperating with ICE, for example. Even the presence of citizens with cameras makes some difference.”

“But there’s not a simple solution to say ‘Let’s just do this thing and keep ICE out of our state entirely,'” she added.

In Biddeford, Guerrero’s killing has revived some community-based efforts that began in January, when ICE initiated an enhanced enforcement operation dubbed “Operation Catch of the Day” in Maine. Woods said she and others have been delivering food and groceries to immigrants scared to leave their homes in the wake of the shooting, as well as providing transportation to bring kids to school and adults to work.

While the city and local officials debate what to do next, she said it’s efforts like those that will hopefully tide an anxious community over until the investigations into Guerrero’s death are completed and ICE ends its aggressive tactics.

“I can’t change the federal government,” Woods said. “But I can help my neighbor.”

text:
ALBANY — Rensselaer County officials said they will defy a new state law that bans congressionally authorized agreements governing immigration enforcement coordination between local, state and federal agencies.

Their latest pledge to defy the statute comes after the attorney general’s office sent letters to 12 local law enforcement agencies across the state last week, including the Rensselaer County Sheriff’s Office, asking the departments to respond by Aug. 14 with the steps they have taken to end the written agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The ban under New York's new statute is scheduled to take effect Aug. 25.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The showdown over the new statute is unfolding as an ongoing legal battle between the state attorney general’s office and the U.S. Department of Justice is pending in U.S. District Court in Albany. The Justice Department argues that the new state statutes intended to restrict local and state agencies from engaging in civil immigration enforcement are unconstitutional, which the attorney general's office disputes.

The formal agreements have for 30 years enabled U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to train local officers to conduct some immigration enforcement duties in exchange for federal funding.

Rensselaer County Sheriff Kyle Bourgault and county Executive Steven McLaughlin said the county will not end their formal agreement with ICE — buttressing statements they have made previously about the law that McLaughlin again on Friday called “illegal.”

Times Union Logo

Don’t miss the next big story

Make the Times Union a Preferred Source on Google to see more of our journalism when you search.

Add Preferred Source

The federal statute that authorizes the agreements — Section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act — was added to the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, which was adopted during the administration of President Bill Clinton. The federal legislation was amended in 2002 to authorize the secretary of the Department of Homeland Security — which was created after the 9/11 terrorist attacks — to enter into written agreements with state and local agencies “so that qualified personnel can perform certain functions of an immigration officer.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Those agreements allow local officers to be deputized to help with detaining migrants targeted for deportation, including making arrests and holding them in county jails, in exchange for federal funding.

The agreements are also part of ICE’s Jail Enforcement Model program. In Rensselaer County, the agreement states it is “designed to identify and process removable aliens” within the county’s correctional facilities.

The agreement says that ICE-trained officers “assigned to detention duties” can process people held at the Rensselaer County jail for immigration violations before transferring them to the custody of the federal agency. The agreement also stipulates that trained officers have the power to interrogate those they believe may be in the country illegally and grants them the authority to collect evidence such as fingerprints, photographs and interviews “for ICE supervisory review.”

The Rensselaer County Sheriff’s Office was for years the only department in the state with a 287(g) agreement. The county's agreement with ICE dates back to 2018 and was renewed in 2020.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Bourgault, in a Friday statement, said the program is “a common-sense effort to ensure anyone wanted on a crime is not released back onto the streets.”

“We are on the right side of the law and we will continue to participate,” Bourgault said.

The letters from the attorney general's office were sent two months after the “Local Cops, Local Crimes Act” was passed by the state Legislature and signed into law by Gov. Kathy Hochul. The act bans 287(g) agreements and voids any of those arrangements already in place. Local law enforcement agencies are not allowed to enter into or extend the federal agreements under the new statutes. State Attorney General Letitia James said the act also prohibits “similar arrangements that use local resources to detain people for federal immigration violations.”

The New York State Sheriffs' Association, which has publicly opposed the measures, noted in recently released guidance that the restrictions under the new laws ban “most state and municipal employees from using public resources, on-duty time, or facilities for immigration enforcement but the ban does not apply to local correctional facilities, nor to local police officers (e.g., sheriffs and deputies), peace officers (or correction officers) … nor their civilian staff.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Bourgault and McLaughlin previously said the county would file a lawsuit to challenge the law.

text:
“Close your eyes,” Lorenzo Salgado Jr. said through measured breaths. His older brother Ronaldo sat, straight-backed, to his right.

On Friday, beneath the bright lights of Harris County’s Commissioners Court, the 27-year-old addressed his words to about a dozen members of the D.C. Democratic brass. The members of the Hispanic congressional caucus and other representatives had flown into Houston all the way from New York, California and Virginia. They were here to hold the Trump administration accountable for the man that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement killed on July 7.

But that morning, Lorenzo Jr. wasn’t just speaking to them. He was also speaking to us. To every American, and all who have followed the details of the senseless death that happened on our street, in our city, in all our names.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“I want you, in your mind, to think of a loved one,” he continued. A brother, perhaps. A father. Or a husband. Even a beloved coworker.

Picture them, with their smile and those eyes that crinkle just so. Say their first and last name in your mind.

Add Preferred Source

And then picture that face, he said.

Pinned to the ground.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Writhing in pain and yelling out in desperate need of help.

“Picture the anger and helplessness of watching that person bleed out through a video on your phone,” Lorenzo Jr. said through gritted teeth. “What would you do after?”

What would you do after the feds – the people you’re supposed to trust – had stolen your “protector, your role model, your mother’s loving partner, your grandmother’s little boy?” When he wasn’t even their target in the first place?

It’s an enraging, heartbreaking scene too many Americans, particularly Black and Hispanic, know far too well. And yet it’s hard to know what any of us would do.

Few but the best of us would be able to summon the Salgado brothers’ graciousness, their adamantine will to resist the ease of despair. Fewer still could forge that will anew each day. But, in the same way that men and women across the country have swallowed their suffocating fear and kept going – getting up before dawn, driving that white van, working until their hands are raw – the brothers do it because they see no other choice.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“You would surely move mountains,” Lorenzo Jr. said. “Go hungry without sleep, marching incessantly towards the slow beating drum of justice.”

It’s that hope – that justice will be served – that has sustained Lorenzo Jr. and Ronnie over the past 17 sleepless days. Speaking at protest after protest, vigil after vigil. Standing before cameras, enduring the ongoing litigation of not just their father’s death but also his life. Knowing that his name and decisions will be dissected on social media, serve as fodder for commenters so cruel you can only hope they’re bots.

It’s also why, despite the media spectacle, they shared their father’s funeral with the entire Houston community, standing by their dad’s open casket for hours into the night, hugging friends and family and shaking strangers’ hands like they were neighbors. To give all of us – all who see even a little bit of ourselves or our loved ones in Lorenzo Salgado Araujo – a chance to grieve.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

They allowed us to see his work boots and construction tools, the ones 52-year-old Lorenzo used over his 35 years here to build homes for other families and a good life for his own.

To see him dancing and dashing and youthful, as young as his sons are now.

To see him. Real and undeniable.

Because the Salgado family has nothing to hide. The United States government, unfortunately, cannot say the same.

No transparency

That was clear at Friday’s hearing, when one elected official after another asked Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare about the ongoing investigation that his office has had to fight just to be able to conduct.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

At every turn, ICE and the Department of Homeland Security have stonewalled Teare’s efforts. They alerted his office to the shooting, as is normal, but didn’t invite his investigators to the scene. They have withheld evidence and moved to deport the three key witnesses. They haven’t shared information about the officer who discharged the fatal shot.

All of it, Teare said, is “unique in its abnormality.” That’s DA-speak for, “This is absurd.”

As an 87-year-old priest from Magnolia Park put it during the hearing, the whole world has turned “insane.” It’s difficult, he added, to work with an administration that has no moral conscience but instead “invincible ignorance.”

Our elected officials, bless their hearts, are trying anyway. U.S. Rep. Sylvia Garcia invited ICE and DHS to attend the hearing and answer urgent questions. Not a single official bothered to show up.

So there was nobody, then – not a single person from the Trump administration – to explain why agents had worn no body cameras when the agency had received millions to buy them, or why an agent had fired shots into a moving vehicle when there was no evidence the officer was forced to do so in self-defense. Much less why the agency released a public statement blaming the victim before any real investigation had even begun.

The American public deserves answers to those basic questions. But the federal government isn’t the only one with much to answer for.

Blame to go around

As U.S. Rep. Joaquin Castro noted, “Texas Governor Greg Abbott is a full partner in that brutality.” Under Abbott’s leadership, we became the first state to send its National Guard to assist in federal detention centers, he said, and compelled state and local law enforcement to assist ICE, despite its recklessness.

For years, our governor exploited immigrants as political pawns, busing them to blue cities while he strung our border with barbed wire and littered the Rio Grande with buoys, all in the name of addressing a dire crisis made worse by the Biden administration’s utter failure to act. Abbott wanted attention, and he got it.

And for what? Now that a man has been killed in his state in the plain light of day, where is his leadership? Where is our Texas delegation, U.S. Sens. Ted Cruz and John Cornyn?

Where is the call – from Republicans as well as Democrats – to reform and rethink immigration, both our laws and their enforcement?

It heartens us to see some congressional members demand accountability. But it’s time for all of Congress to take responsibility for its part in this tragedy. Lorenzo’s death was the preventable result of decades of dawdling on immigration reform, of doubling down on ruthless deterrence without addressing the lack of legal pathways to meet American employers’ needs. Their inaction has left vulnerable millions of immigrants and the cities they call home.

When Lorenzo Salgado Araujo died, something else died with him: Many Americans’ trust in their government. We can’t let his legacy end there. The same way Lorenzo helped build this city with his own two hands, his memory can help us build something better – a humane and commonsense immigration system worthy of this country’s ideals.

It’ll take courage, dogged and unrelenting. The kind shown by Rep. Sylvia Garcia, as Ronnie recalled, when, “in her powerful pink suit jacket,” she demanded to speak with the higher-ups at Ben Taub Hospital. To help him confirm that his father had, indeed, died.

On Friday, Garcia promised the hearing wouldn’t end there. “We are stronger than fear,” she said, her voice thick with emotion. “We are stronger than intimidation. We will keep fighting until justice is done.”

Through their extraordinary resolve, Ronnie and Lorenzo Jr. have shown us what is possible. They’ve made Houston – and the entire country – proud. It’s time we made them proud too.

text:
WASHINGTON — A new briefing from the Prison Policy Initiative argues that the Trump administration’s expansion of immigration enforcement is driving a rapid increase in federal incarceration, detention and surveillance, while a growing network of federal agencies is expanding the reach of the nation’s criminal legal system. The report contends that understanding those systems is essential to holding the federal government accountable and informing future policy decisions.

The briefing examines the agencies, policies and detention systems that make up the federal correctional apparatus, arguing that changes implemented since 2024 have reshaped how people are detained, prosecuted and supervised. According to PPI, those shifts have made it increasingly difficult for the public to understand which agencies are responsible for expanding confinement.

PPI begins by examining the growing rate of federal confinement in the United States. According to the briefing, the number of people confined by the federal government has increased by 631%. While that figure remains below the all-time peak reached in 2011, federal incarceration and detention rates have increased by 12% during the past two years.

With particular attention to deportation and mass detention, the briefing argues that the Trump administration has fundamentally reshaped the federal system through changes in immigration enforcement, policing and prosecution. Even from a broad perspective, the report says, it can be difficult to identify those changes, determine which agencies are responsible and understand how they have affected incarceration since 2024.

The briefing encourages the public to examine the federal system more closely, arguing that a better understanding of its mechanisms will help state and local governments push back against federal overreach.

According to the briefing, 268,000 people are currently detained or incarcerated, while another 321,000 people face the threat of confinement through federal supervision. Combined, those figures represent more than half a million people under some form of federal correctional control across four agencies, multiple charges and a range of pending legal statuses.

The briefing explains that after a federal arrest, there are three primary pathways into confinement: pretrial detention while a case proceeds through court, which it argues often prevents the accused from securing release on bail; a sentence of incarceration; or detention by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement while a civil immigration case proceeds or while an individual awaits deportation.

Many people who do not fall into one of those three categories nevertheless remain under community supervision. According to the briefing, agencies involved at each stage of the legal process routinely share resources to detain, incarcerate and supervise people with criminal convictions.

Regarding incarceration, the briefing states that many people serving short federal sentences remain in the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service instead of being transferred to a federal prison. It claims that “1 in 5 people serving a federal sentence of incarceration on any given day are in USMS custody” and notes that the Federal Bureau of Prisons is responsible for managing people serving federal incarceration sentences.

The Bureau of Prisons oversees prison camps, penitentiaries, detention centers and correctional institutions. According to the briefing, the agency is responsible for incarcerating or detaining 25% of the federal population, and 55% of those individuals remain under either total confinement or supervision.

Immigration detention follows a different pathway, with federal civil immigration cases potentially resulting in detention at ICE facilities. According to the briefing, those detention networks include privately operated prisons, federal detention centers, ICE facilities, state prisons and Bureau of Prisons institutions. It also highlights the relationship between ICE and the U.S. Marshals Service, saying it gives ICE direct access to local jails through intergovernmental agreements.

The U.S. Marshals Service alone currently holds 5% of all detained or incarcerated people, according to the briefing.

Community supervision also extends federal control beyond incarceration, the report argues, through pretrial supervision, probation and post-release monitoring. Beyond those who are incarcerated, the briefing states that 321,000 people remain under federal supervision and face potential confinement for violations. That supervision is managed by the federal courts’ Probation and Pretrial Services.

The report argues that immigrant criminalization has become the primary driver of federal confinement. According to the briefing, detention in immigration facilities has continued to grow under President Donald Trump and is expected to expand significantly as Congress increases funding and detention capacity.

Moreover, with congressional approval to roughly double detention capacity, the briefing projects that federal confinement will soon reach an all-time high.

While ICE expansion has drawn the greatest public attention, the briefing argues that the U.S. Marshals Service and the Bureau of Prisons have also played major but often overlooked roles in expanding detention related to immigration enforcement.

According to the briefing, matters that were once handled as civil immigration cases increasingly involve criminal detention and incarceration because of the expanded role of those agencies. It argues that immigration arrests and detentions have extended into jurisdictions with sanctuary policies because of what it describes as a longstanding loophole.

The briefing explains that “ICE and other federal agencies can refer people for federal prosecution on immigration-related ‘crimes’ and thus hold them in contracted local jails in sanctuary cities, counties, and states.” It argues that this practice has transformed civil immigration matters into federal criminal prosecutions, contributing to the expansion of federal incarceration.

The report further states that “every county with a U.S. Marshal’s contract is effectively signed up for this part of the mass detention and deportation agenda, even if they have sanctuary policies on their books,” arguing that the practice is well understood within government but far less understood by the public.

According to PPI estimates, roughly 25,000 people were detained or incarcerated on immigration-related criminal charges on average during 2025. The briefing points to federal prosecutors filing more immigration-related criminal cases, sending increasing numbers of people into the criminal legal system.

The briefing states that “almost 50,000 people were charged and booked into the U.S. Marshal’s custody for an immigration-related offense in fiscal year 2025 alone.” It also notes that the administration projects booking another 250,000 people into jail during fiscal year 2027, compared with fewer than 100,000 federal bookings in 2024.

Among those projections, the briefing identifies the “expected booking of almost 110,000 people on immigration-related criminal charges, followed by sharp increases in the catch-all ‘other charges’ group,” which it says historically has included supervision violations and property offenses.

Beyond immigration detention, the briefing states that the Trump administration also plans a rapid increase in the number of people booked on federal drug charges. It argues those changes will result in more people accused of drug offenses being held in pretrial detention for longer periods and will “exacerbate the harmful impacts of pretrial detention in the federal system.”

According to the briefing, those policies create burdens for the accused, court personnel and the judicial system while also imposing substantial financial costs. It estimates that ICE detention alone costs an average of $222 per person per day.

Beyond financial costs, the briefing also points to increasing reports about conditions in ICE detention facilities, citing allegations of “abuse and cruelty, inedible food, and medical neglect.”

PPI argues that detention at its current scale represents government waste. The briefing contends that a better use of public resources would be to “release people on recognizance at no financial cost,” allowing immigration and criminal courts to pursue less expensive alternatives to detention.

The briefing states that while alternatives to detention remain restrictive and can include “electronic monitoring,” they nevertheless “keep people from [detention’s] worst harm.”

The report also identifies a lack of current and comprehensive federal data as a major obstacle to accountability. It states that while the Bureau of Justice Statistics publishes annual reports on state and federal prison populations, those reports omit the 32,000 people serving federal sentences while held by the U.S. Marshals Service.

According to the briefing, ICE also regularly fails to publish “congressionally mandated semi-monthly reports summarizing statistics on detention over the past year,” making it more difficult to understand the true scope of federal detention.

The briefing argues that those reporting gaps make it harder to hold agencies accountable. For example, it notes that the government only occasionally releases information about the charges faced by people held in pretrial detention.

It also states that “academic research [had] shown that many judges grant prosecutors’ requests to detain defendants even when there is no legal basis and, legally, these defendants should be granted pretrial release on the ‘least restrictive means available’.” According to the briefing, reduced reporting now prevents researchers from tracking those trends over time.

The briefing concludes that the United States incarcerates and detains “far more” people than comparable nations and argues that policymakers have direct authority over laws, budgets and the confirmation of agency directors and judges.

It concludes that addressing the expansion of federal confinement should be a central policy priority. With the continued criminalization of immigration and the ongoing “war on drugs,” the report argues that further expansion of federal detention deserves heightened public scrutiny.

The briefing closes by encouraging state and local governments to act, stating that “while federal policy action is essential to changing this system and reversing its buildup, states and local governments can take steps now.”

Ultimately, the briefing argues that understanding how federal agencies operate is essential to holding the federal government accountable and shaping future policy decisions.

text:
More than 330,000 Haitian immigrants in the US are set to lose their ability to legally live and work in the country as the Trump administration seeks to terminate their temporary protected status. An estimated 13,000 are nursing assistants, who care for 65,000 patients every day.

“I get up at 5am every morning and I take two buses to work to clean the rooms of the residents. I give my heart,” said a nursing home housekeeper with TPS from Haiti, who requested to remain anonymous for fear of retaliation. “These residents are like my grandmother.”

“I want to stay here in New York where I can be safe and care for my residents,” they added. “I cannot return to Haiti. It is not safe. I’m afraid that I would be killed if I return.”

Donald Trump’s officials take a different view. The US supreme court ruled 6 to 3 in favor of the administration’s efforts to terminate TPS from Haitians and Syrians in June.

As tens of thousands of Haitian immigrants prepare to lose their protections, families, communities and industries across the US are braced for extraordinary upheaval.

“The impact is not just for the TPS recipients, but our whole communities,” said Roxana Rivera, assistant to the president at Service Employees International Union (SEIU) 32BJ. The union represents thousands of immigrant workers with TPS.

“We do think this is a racist act from the administration targeting immigrants,” said Rivera.

Homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin has argued immigrants with TPS should leave the US and seek other legal immigration statuses – despite no direct pathway from TPS to a green card, and asylum grant rates under the Trump administration having plummeted to less than 5%.

The US state department has currently issued a non-travel advisory for Haiti due to a national state of emergency, as the country remains unsafe. TPS was first designated for Haitians in 2010.

“The vast displacement of folks that have been law-abiding citizens being abruptly pulled and uprooted, basically losing employment, not being able to work, but also facing deportation and detention to home countries that are unsafe, is of a huge impact for our members and their workplaces,” added Rivera. “In the service sector, they can’t operate without immigrant workers, and they already have a hard time filling vacancies because of turnover.”

A second immigrant from Haiti, based in New York, Pierre Etienne, who is a US citizen but has family members and friends in the US with TPS, criticized the decision to end the protections.

“I have family members and close friends who are protected under TPS. They left Haiti because their lives were in danger. Armed gangs took over their neighborhoods, forcing them to flee and leaving them without their homes and everything they had built,” said Etienne. “They would be returning to a country where many areas remain unsafe and where they may have nowhere to live or no way to support themselves. Knowing that my loved ones could be placed in harm’s way causes me tremendous fear, stress and anxiety.”

A third immigrant from Haiti, based in New York, who has lived in the US since 2000 and requested to remain anonymous for fear of retaliation, told of how the termination of his temporary protected status had upended his life.

“The loss of TPS and my work authorization has turned my family’s life upside down,” he said. “This is where I became an adult, established my life, worked, paid taxes and built my family. I am married, and I am the father of two daughters who were born in the United States.”

He and other Haitian immigrants with TPS did everything right, he said: registering, completing background checks, paying application fees and document renewals and organizing their lives around the protections.

Now, he is set to lose his ability to legally work, but the bills for food, housing, utilities and caring for his children remain.

“I’m not asking for special treatment. I’m asking for a fair opportunity to continue supporting my family and contributing to the country that has been my home since 2000,” he added. “It also creates the constant fear that I could be separated from my family and sent to a country that I left more than 25 years ago.

“My daughters are Americans, but they now have to live with the possibility that their father may not be allowed to remain with them.”

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security claimed conditions in Haiti have improved enough to support the return of Haitians, despite the ongoing US travel advisory and the United Nations warning that the country continues to be plagued by violence.

They did not respond to criticism that ending TPS for Haitians would be a mistake and cause labor disruptions to industries and employers reliant on Haitian immigrants.

“Temporary Protected Status is exactly that – temporary,” the spokesperson said. “For too long, TPS has been allowed to function as a de facto amnesty program despite Congress never intending it to be permanent.”

A White House spokesperson added that TPS “was never intended to be a pathway to permanent status or legal residency”.

The second Haitian worker also criticized the hateful rhetoric toward immigrants from elected officials in recent years, including the false claim from Trump during his 2024 presidential campaign that Haitian immigrants were eating pets in Springfield, Ohio.

“Haitians should not be judged by stereotypes or used as political targets,” he said. “We’re human beings, parents, workers, taxpayers, neighbors and members of American communities.

“When political leaders make degrading or misleading statements about an entire community, those statements have real consequences. They create fear, discrimination, workplace hostility, bullying of Haitian children and sometimes even threats of violence.”

title: ICE plans to target Haitians as Temporary Protected Status is set to end, sources say
description:
The internal plans for a potential arrest and deportation blitz have been made as more than 300,000 Haitians prepare to lose deportation protections and work permits under the Temporary Protected Status, or TPS, program.
The Supreme Court last month sided with the Trump administration in its efforts to end the TPS programs for Haitians and Syrians.
The ICE sources who described the preparations requested anonymity to describe internal plans that have not been publicly disclosed and are fluid.
The Trump administration moved to end the Haiti TPS policy last year, but the decision has been held up in court ever since.
Last month, the number of detainees booked into ICE custody hit a monthly record high for the second Trump administration.
text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has made plans to ramp up operations to arrest and deport Haitian migrants, as hundreds of thousands of Haitians brace for the termination of their legal status, according to two agency sources and federal documents obtained by CBS News.

The plans include arresting migrants in Ohio — where large Haitian communities in cities like Springfield have been targeted by President Trump and conservative politicians and commentators — and quickly putting them on deportation flights to crisis-stricken Haiti, the internal documents indicate. During the 2024 presidential campaign, Mr. Trump amplified baseless claims that Haitians in Springfield were eating cats and dogs.

The internal plans for a potential arrest and deportation blitz have been made as more than 300,000 Haitians prepare to lose deportation protections and work permits under the Temporary Protected Status, or TPS, program. The Supreme Court last month sided with the Trump administration in its efforts to end the TPS programs for Haitians and Syrians. That ruling's binding mandate is set to be issued to lower courts on Monday.

Since that ruling, fear and uncertainty have swept throughout Haitian communities across the U.S. Immigrants whose TPS lapses immediately lose their ability to work in the country legally, and become eligible to be arrested and processed for deportation by ICE, unless they have another status. Those without removal orders are generally entitled to appear before an immigration judge before any deportation can take place.

The operations targeting Haitian migrants could start as early as this week, the documents suggest, but more details about the scale of the plans were not immediately clear. The ICE sources who described the preparations requested anonymity to describe internal plans that have not been publicly disclosed and are fluid.

Any uptick in deportations to Haiti would almost certainly raise political and humanitarian challenges, given the dire situation in the Caribbean nation, the poorest country in the Western Hemisphere. Significant portions of Haiti are controlled by criminal gangs, and the U.S. has generally limited deportations to Cap-Haïtien, in the country's north, due to the instability and insecurity in the capital of Port-au-Prince. The State Department urges Americans not to visit Haiti under any circumstances, citing the rampant violence there.

In a statement to CBS News, the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, said it "does not discuss ongoing or future operations." It argued TPS has been used as a "defacto amnesty program" and suggested that those set to lose their status should self-deport.

"What we would say now is it's closing time which means you don't have to go home, but you can't stay here," DHS added in its statement. "The good news is it's not too late to get a $2,600 check and a free flight home."

Created in 1990 by Congress, TPS allows federal immigration officials to grant temporary work permits and a reprieve from deportation to immigrants from countries facing an armed conflict, environmental disaster or another emergency.

The Trump administration has sought to end most TPS programs, arguing that they incentivize illegal immigration and that they have been unnecessarily extended for too long by Democratic administrations, despite the temporary nature of the policy. It has terminated or moved to end TPS programs for hundreds of thousands of immigrants from Afghanistan, Cameroon, Honduras, Nicaragua, Venezuela and other countries.

A version of Haiti's TPS program has been around since 2010, following the devastating earthquake there that year. But most of those currently enrolled in the program came to the U.S. under the Biden administration, either illegally along the southern border or through programs, since terminated by Mr. Trump's White House, that allowed Haitians and other immigrants to enter the country legally.

The Trump administration moved to end the Haiti TPS policy last year, but the decision has been held up in court ever since.

In a ruling in February, U.S. District Court Judge Ana Reyes found that the move to end the program was "in part" rooted in "racial animus," citing disparaging remarks that then DHS Secretary Kristi Noem and Mr. Trump made about Haiti and immigrants. But in its decision last month, the Supreme Court's majority said federal law barred judges from reviewing TPS determinations and found Mr. Trump's comments not to be "overtly racial."

The Trump administration scaled back large-scale immigration roundups after two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were killed by federal agents during a massive deployment to the Minneapolis area in January. But ICE operations have ramped up this summer, amid pressure for the agency to record 2,000 daily arrests.

Last month, the number of detainees booked into ICE custody hit a monthly record high for the second Trump administration. During the recent surge in ICE operations, two immigrants from Mexico and Colombia were killed by agents during traffic stops in Texas and Maine.

text:
A federal judge ruled that an Illinois law allowing some undocumented immigrants to pay in-state tuition rates to attend the state’s public colleges and universities is unconstitutional.

What we know:

The ruling stemmed from a lawsuit brought by the U.S. Attorney’s Office in the Southern District of Illinois and U.S. Department of Justice’s Civil Division last year.

Judge David W. Dugan ruled that Illinois allowing undocumented immigrants to pay in-state tuition at its public colleges and universities was "unconstitutional and invalid."

Dugan ruled similarly on the Retention of Illinois Students & Equity (RISE) Act, which gives undocumented college students access to state financial aid. In order to qualify, a student must have graduated from an Illinois high school and attended an in-state school for at least three years, and pledge to file an application to become a permanent U.S. resident as soon as they are eligible.

"Illinois sought to incentivize illegal immigration on the taxpayer’s dime by treating illegal aliens better than U.S. citizens living in other states, in clear violation of federal law," said U.S. Attorney Steven D. Weinhoeft, in a statement. "This ruling enforces the statute Congress wrote and stops the State from putting illegal aliens ahead of American citizens."

The lawsuit named Gov. JB Pritzker, Attorney General Kwame Raoul and officials from several state colleges including Southern Illinois University, Rend Lake College, the University of Illinois, Chicago State University, Eastern Illinois University, Illinois State University, and Northeastern Illinois University.

What we don't know:

Spokespeople for Pritzker and Raoul did not immediately respond to requests for comment or about whether they would appeal the decision.

text:
The sounds of horns filled the Route 1 corridor in Hyattsville on Saturday as drivers supported a vigil to remember people killed during encounters with ICE agents.

The observance, organized by Indivisible Route 1 Corridor, brought together immigrant rights groups, faith leaders and residents calling for accountability and support for affected families.

“We get a lot of public support when we do an event like this,” said Laura Usher, co-leader of Indivisible Route 1 Corridor.

“We’re really grateful to have the support of the faith community in speaking out against the reprehensible treatment of immigrants.”

One of the signs held along the sidewalk read, “ICE agents repent, love, and save your souls.” Its owner, 20-year-old Jenifer Pineda, said fear has shaped her life and the lives of other children of immigrants.

“Before, it was, we couldn’t go outside because of COVID, and I was like, we can’t go outside because of the fear of our parents being taken away,” she said.

Pineda, president of the youth group at St. Matthew’s Episcopal Church, said her uncle was detained last August on his way to work, forcing her aunt and young cousin to leave the country.

Karen Murphy, who began protesting with her parents during the Vietnam War era, was joined Saturday by her son and daughter.

“I need to see more people at events like this,” she said. “Put down your phones and join these events.” She added,

“This isn’t right. This isn’t America. We stand up for human rights. This is a country of immigrants.”

Maryland Rep. Glenn Ivey told WTOP that ICE agents are being asked to do work they are not trained for.

“These ICE agents aren’t trained to be doing the work that the administration has them doing,” he said.

“They really should be using these agents to focus on finding the worst of the worst instead of these roving patrols and racial profiling stops.”

The vigil included prayers, songs led by the Rapid Response Choir, and a reading of the names of people killed in ICE encounters. Organizers also collected food for Route 1 Mutual Aid, which supports families affected by ICE detentions.

description:

But at the State House, measures to cancel Wyatt's ICE contract — Senate Bill 2278 and House Bill 7436 — stalled in the Senate Judiciary Committee.

text:
It appears that the federal government has stopped telling the public what its immigration machine is actually doing — and Rhode Island, home to New England's primary detention hub and roughly 175,000 immigrants, is left to take the Trump administration's word for it.

ICE has not released its semimonthly "Detention Management" report on arrests, detentions and deportations since April 9, 2026, when the agency reported holding more than 60,000 people in custody. The gap — now stretching past three months — is the longest since Congress mandated the reports in 2020, according to reporting first published by The Marshall Project. For six years the agency largely complied with that congressional requirement, with only short delays, including one last fall during a prolonged government shutdown. This blackout is different.

Into that silence, the White House has poured big numbers. The administration claims it has deported more than 605,000 people, with an additional 1.9 million "self-deporting," for a total of more than 2.5 million who have left the country since President Trump returned to office. In an email, the Department of Homeland Security told The Marshall Project that, through June 24, the administration had arrested more than 981,000 people and deported 948,000.

Local sponsorWorld-class website design at a small business priceCompany 50

The independent record does not match the rhetoric. Analysis by the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse at Syracuse University puts total removals during the Trump administration at 290,603 — just 7 percent more than were removed in the last full year of the Biden administration, despite the enormous increase in money and personnel poured into enforcement. The administration has never explained how it defines or tracks the 1.9 million it counts as "self-deportations."

"It's important for us to know what our government is doing, especially in the Trump administration, which is known for its fabulism," said Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, a senior fellow at the American Immigration Council. The demand for the data cuts across the political spectrum: at least three lawsuits are pending, including one filed July 8 by the conservative Oversight Project seeking what it calls the "true deportation statistics." The Deportation Data Project, run out of UC Berkeley and UCLA, has also sued, with The Marshall Project filing an amicus brief.

What the missing reports would clarify matters directly in Rhode Island. The Donald W. Wyatt Detention Facility in Central Falls is the state's only ICE detention site and functions as the de facto holding hub for New England — people arrested by ICE across the Boston Area of Responsibility, including sanctuary states with no detention of their own, are routinely held at Wyatt while their cases proceed. The facility listed 102 ICE detainees as of April 28.

Even as removals lag, detention has exploded. The daily immigration detention population hit a record of more than 73,400 people on a single day in mid-January 2026, and populations on every day since mid-June 2025 have exceeded the previous peak set in August 2019. The administration insists it is targeting "the worst of the worst." The data says otherwise: as of April 4, 42,722 of the 60,311 people in ICE custody — 70.8 percent — had no criminal conviction, and more than one in three people deported from detention in 2025 had no criminal record at all.

Rhode Island officials have already felt ICE's reach up close. On Nov. 20, 2025, a high school student interning for Providence County Superior Court Judge Joseph McBurney was detained by ICE outside the Licht Judicial Complex in Providence. Confronting Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem on March 4, U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse said of the arrest, "There was nothing professional about that entire exchange."

The state's response has been uneven. Providence Mayor Brett Smiley signed an executive order on Jan. 20 barring federal immigration officers from city property and directing that police not act as immigration agents. But at the State House, measures to cancel Wyatt's ICE contract — Senate Bill 2278 and House Bill 7436 — stalled in the Senate Judiciary Committee. Complicating any push to close the facility, the Central Falls Detention Facility Corporation, which operates Wyatt, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on July 13 with a plan to keep operating, and in May made a $250,000 host-fee payment to Central Falls — its first since 2021.

"As part of good governance, ICE should be reporting this basic data," said Heidi Altman, vice president of policy at the National Immigration Law Center. Until it does, the people held in Central Falls, and the families waiting for word about them, are counting on numbers no one outside the agency can see.

text:
Federal immigration officials confirmed they have deported former Indianapolis Colts linebacker Daniel Adongo, the Kenyan rugby convert whose signing in 2013 was one of the more unusual roster experiments in recent NFL history. It caps a decade in which he cycled through arrests, courtrooms and psychiatric hospitals.

Adongo, 37, was removed from the United States on June 20 after a Justice Department immigration judge ordered his removal in March, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement confirmed Saturday. He had been in custody for months. ICE said he overstayed his visa in 2016, the year after his football career ended, and that he was held without bond under the Laken Riley Act. The department described him as a "dangerous" individual.

"Those who violate immigration law are held equally accountable, including former professional athletes," ICE Chicago assistant field office director Douglas Thompson said in a statement.

USA TODAY reached out to ICE for comment on where Adongo was deported to.

Adongo has one conviction, a Class A misdemeanor for criminal mischief in 2020 and was sentenced to 364 days in jail, according to ICE. Other arrests for intimidation, battery and disorderly conduct had charges dismissed.

Court records reviewed by the Indianapolis Star, part of the USA TODAY Network, show that judges twice found Adongo incompetent to stand trial. In one filing, Dr. Jason Jaronik wrote that Adongo was acutely psychotic and raised the possibility of a traumatic brain injury from his playing days.

His mother, Betty Adongo, asked the court to release her son for medical evaluation. Family and social workers have said they believe his illness is tied to injuries he suffered as an athlete. No such link can be confirmed in a living patient.

Attempts to contact Betty Adongo were not immediately successful Saturday.

Adongo was 23 and playing Super Rugby in South Africa when Colts general manager Ryan Grigson signed him in July 2013. He had never watched a football game. The team spent a season teaching him the sport on the practice field.

He appeared in five games over three seasons and played one defensive snap. He earned roughly $694,000.

Indianapolis waived him in December 2015, a week after police were called to his home over a reported domestic disturbance. It was the second call in two months. No charges were filed in either case.

text:
International Relations Minister Ronald Lamola says South Africa’s migration challenges must be addressed through cooperation, not blame.

Image: Leon Lestrade/Independent Newspapers

International Relations and Cooperation Minister Ronald Lamola says poverty, unemployment and inequality are the real drivers of social frustration, and has rejected claims that migrants are to blame for all of South Africa’s social and economic problems.

He made the remarks at the Kgalema Motlanthe Foundation’s winter seminar in Sandton on Thursday, where discussions focused on migration.

His comments come as anti-migrant groups continue to call for undocumented foreign nationals to leave South Africa, despite repeated government appeals for calm.

Lamola emphasised the importance of the seminar, saying the migration-related challenges facing South Africa require platforms where difficult questions can be debated honestly, respectfully and constructively.

"Indeed, the current wave of discussions around migration, border management, social cohesion, economic competition, and public service delivery has generated intense public debate."

Poverty, not migration, is the real crisis

He said the issues confronting the country are complex, perspectives are firmly held and emotions often run deep.

"That is why platforms such as this are essential to fostering meaningful dialogue. We have not gathered here to impose predetermined answers or reinforce existing positions.

"The objective should be about providing a platform for deliberate engagement, fruitful discourse, and critical thinking."

Lamola said migration is not a new phenomenon.

"People throughout human history have moved in search of safety, opportunity, family reunification, and a better future.

"At the same time, migration has often raised legitimate questions about governance, resource allocation, identity, and social integration."

Ronald Lamola has called for a balanced approach to migration, saying South Africa must address community concerns while protecting human rights and strengthening regional cooperation.

Image: File

Communities have legitimate concerns

He argued that South Africa's history has been shaped by movement, displacement, the struggle for human dignity, solidarity, and experiencing exclusion.

"The birth of our constitutional democracy was rooted in the commitment to human rights, equality, and the recognition of our common humanity."

However, he said it would be disingenuous to ignore the realities faced by many communities.

"High levels of poverty, unemployment and inequality continue to put significant stress on households and communities.

"Jobs, housing, education, health care and other public services are often scarce commodities and the feeling that they are not available to all fuels exclusionary politics.

"In such contexts, migrants are likely to be the target of wider frustrations associated with structural socio-economic problems," Lamola said.

Migration is an African challenge

He said the country must approach the migration debate with honesty and nuance.

"On the one hand, we must resist simple narratives that seek to blame migrants for all our social and economic problems."

The minister said such perspectives ignore the complexities of developmental challenges and are likely to increase intolerance and social division.

"On the other hand, we need to recognise the legitimate concerns of communities about the effective management of immigration, border security, the regulation of labour markets and the capacity of public institutions.

"To dismiss these fears is not to forge social cohesion but to undermine public trust. The challenge before us is not whether to choose between security and humanity or national interests and human rights."

According to Lamola, the real challenge is implementing policies that promote all of these objectives simultaneously.

"This means that decisions about policy should be based on facts, not on feelings. Effective and fair migration management requires strong institutions.

Facts over fear

"It urges African nations to collaborate to address migration drivers like conflict, political instability, unemployment, inequality, and climate change.

"Most importantly, it requires an acceptance that migration cannot be considered in isolation from wider development issues."

He argued that the movement of people is often a symptom of deeper economic, political and social conditions.

"To get to sustainable, long-term solutions, we really have to address those underlying drivers."

Lamola said the purpose of the seminar was not necessarily to achieve complete consensus.

"Indeed, reasonable people will disagree on many aspects of migration policy.

"Our willingness to engage with one another honestly, to test our assumptions, and to deepen our collective understanding of the issues is of greater value, as it enables us to progress from rhetoric to practical solutions."

Speaking on possible solutions, Lamola said South Africa cannot address migration challenges on its own.

"What we need to understand is that the migration challenge confronting South Africa cannot be addressed through South African solutions alone. Addressing this issue requires solutions that are specifically tailored to the realities of Africa.

"It is not feasible or sustainable to consider migration only from a national perspective. We need to strengthen regional cooperation, step up economic integration, and work together to create opportunities across the African continent."

International Relations and Cooperation Minister Ronald Lamola says poverty, unemployment and inequality are the real drivers of social frustration, warning against narratives that blame migrants for the country’s challenges.

Image: Doctor Ngcobo/ ANA Studio

Lamola said the prosperity and stability of African countries are interconnected.

"We must recognise that the prosperity and stability of one African nation are intrinsically linked to the prosperity and stability of others.

"As Africans, we share a common history, a common destiny, and, increasingly, common challenges.

"The question before us is not simply how SouthAfrica manages migration but how Africa creates the conditions under which migration becomes a matter of choice rather than necessity."

He said Africa must move beyond narrow national responses.

"Our challenge is to look beyond narrow national responses and toward a continental conversation based on solidarity, shared responsibility, and a commitment to inclusive development.

“Only then will we have the chance to develop solutions that are effective and sustainable and just.

"In the current context, it is for the benefit of our great continent, Africa, that we come together to examine the issue of migration into South Africa not merely as a South African challenge but as an African challenge."

Lamola said South Africa has experienced increasing migration from several African countries, particularly Southern African Development Community (SADC) member states, including Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Lesotho and Malawi.

Secure borders and human rights can coexist

According to him, migration is driven by economic opportunities, political and governance challenges, environmental factors, and enduring family and cultural ties across borders.

"This reality presents the critical question: how do we as leaders and citizens of the SADC region work together to address the conditions that compel people to leave their countries of origin?

“How do we grow our economies, deepen regional integration, and create opportunities that allow our people to thrive in their own communities if they want to?"

He called on SADC member states to increase cooperation and engage in honest discussions on economic development, youth unemployment, governance, skills mobility and regional investment.

"It is important to tackle the root causes of migration, not just migration management.

"Let me put it very clearly: South Africa remains committed to the ideals of Pan-Africanism, and we continue to welcome our brothers and sisters from across the continent.

"Our history is a reminder of the importance of solidarity, and we thank many African countries who stood with us in our struggle for freedom."

However, Lamola said social cohesion and public confidence in migration depend on a legal and orderly framework.

Rejecting vigilantism

"We need to have proper and secure management of the migration flows, processing documentation efficiently, protecting the rights of migrants and enforcing immigration laws fairly and consistently.

"We should therefore not look to divide Africans or create animosity towards migrants. Rather, our objective should be to build a migration system that is humane, well-managed, and responsive to the legitimate concerns of both host communities and migrants themselves."

"We will not build the future we seek through isolation but through partnership; not through blame but through cooperation; not through division but through a shared commitment to building a prosperous, stable, and integrated Africa."

He said only then can migration become a source of opportunity rather than tension.

"The question often asked is: What is the SouthAfrican Police Service or Government doing to combat illegal immigration and to manage the tensions arising from migration-related protests?"

Lamola said the government continues to strengthen migration management through coordinated efforts involving the South African Police Service, theDepartment of Home Affairs and the Border Management Authority.

"These interventions include enforcement operations, improved border management and stronger action against immigration-related criminal activity.

"While citizens have the constitutional right to protest peacefully, the enforcement of immigration laws remains the responsibility of the State.

"This reflects a core value of our constitutional democracy: worries about illegal immigration are legitimate issues for public debate and government action, but they must be addressed lawfully and democratically, not through vigilante justice or hostility toward migrants."

According to Lamola, police have maintained a visible presence during migration-related demonstrations to prevent violence, intimidation,vigilantism and attacks on foreign nationals.

However, during the nationwide protests against undocumented immigrants on June 30, some people were arrested for public violence.

The National Joint Operational and IntelligenceStructure (NatJoints) previously said more than 900 people were arrested during the demonstrations, with the majority being undocumented foreign nationals.

Some were arrested for public violence, others for harbouring undocumented immigrants, and others for business robberies at spaza shops.

"We need to assist law enforcement agencies in carrying out their duties and address the root causes of migration through regional cooperation, economic development, and stronger partnerships among SADC member states.

“In the end, secure borders, effective migration management and African solidarity are not mutually exclusive goals, but complementary pillars of a stable and prosperous region."

Lamola insisted South Africans are not xenophobic.

"South Africans are not inherently xenophobic; they are a welcoming and Pan-Africanist people. Our country remains open to legal immigrants," he added.

text:
A coalition of privacy and civil liberties advocates filed a federal lawsuit Friday accusing the Trump administration of secretly collecting and keeping personal information about people who monitor US Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations, arguing that the practice violates federal privacy law and threatens constitutionally protected speech and association.

The lawsuit—filed in the US District Court for the District of Columbia—was brought by individuals and advocacy groups represented by Democracy Forward.

The plaintiffs—the Electronic Privacy Information Center (EPIC) and legal observers Nicole Cleland, Jacquelyn Ivey, and Anna Walker—argued that the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and other federal agencies created and maintained databases of people who observed, documented, or protested immigration enforcement activities without providing notification or safeguards, as required under the Privacy Act of 1974.

That law was passed after the exposure of illegal government surveillance, including longtime former Federal Bureau of Investigation Director J. Edgar Hoover's infamous COINTELPRO program, under which the FBI, in addition to conducting unlawful spying, funded and armed murderous far-right militants to terrorize anti-Vietnam War protesters, anti-nuclear weapons activists, civil rights leaders including Martin Luther King, Jr., and other leftists.

“The federal government cannot build secret dossiers on people because they exercise their First Amendment right to peacefully observe, document, or criticize its actions," Democracy Forward president and CEO Skye Perryman said in a statement announcing the lawsuit. "That is exactly the kind of government surveillance Congress sought to prevent when it enacted the Privacy Act after some of the darkest chapters in our nation’s history."

The lawsuit accuses the Trump administration of collecting the names, photographs, vehicle information and license plate numbers, social media accounts, and other identifying information about legal observers, volunteers, journalists, clergy, and community members engaged in First Amendment-protected activities during the government's deadly anti-immigrant crackdown.

"When the Department of Homeland Security dramatically ratcheted up its immigration enforcement, people across the country—of all ages and backgrounds—did what anyone is supposed to do when they disagree with government action: They exercised their First Amendment rights," the suit states. "They peacefully protested. And, as matters here, they observed and recorded how law enforcement agents acted in public."

"In response, DHS decided to record the Americans who were peacefully observing its agents, adopting a secret Protester Surveillance Policy enabling its agents to first collect records on Americans engaging in First Amendment exercise and then maintain them in DHS systems, where they can be used to retaliate against those Americans," the complaint continues.

"Beginning sometime in 2025, DHS deployed a dragnet of drones, bodycams, face-scanning apps, license plate scanners, and camera phones to, as one memo instructed, 'capture all images, license plates, identifications, and general information on hotels, agitators, protestors, etc., so we can capture it all in one consolidated form,'" the document notes.

"DHS agents have not been shy about gathering this information or its purpose," the plaintiffs contended. "In Maine, DHS agents told multiple observers that they were being added to a database of 'domestic terrorists.' In Chicago, agents routinely used facial irecognition scans on members of the public."

"In Minneapolis, observers simply watching agents on public streets have been led by those agents to their own houses, despite never having interacted with an agent—a practice so common that it has been named 'being driven home by ICE,'" the suit says. "And across the country, DHS agents have approached observers and addressed them by their full names, even though those observers never identified themselves to the agents or showed them any form of identification."

"As a result of its Protester Surveillance Policy, DHS has recorded and retaliated against each individual plaintiff," the filing alleges. "It’s bad enough that DHS publicly collected information on Americans engaged in lawful First Amendment exercise. But worse, DHS also decided to maintain the information in one or more of its systems, enabling it to later retaliate against observers and protestors—including by canceling Trusted Traveler status," which includes Transportation Security Administration Pre-Check and Global Entry.

The plaintiffs are asking the court to declare the DHS surveillance policy unlawful, end it, and ban the agency from continuing to collect and keep records of individuals’ protected First Amendment activities.

“Now more than ever, those of us who have the privilege to speak out have a responsibility to defend the rights of everyone in our communities,” Walker said in a statement. “When people are punished for exercising their First Amendment rights, we begin losing the democratic principles that protect all of us. Every American should be alarmed by retaliatory action against one’s free speech."

Cleland said: “I believe government accountability starts with transparency. People should be free to peacefully observe and document what their government does in public without worrying they’ll be tracked or retaliated against. This case is about protecting that right for everyone.”

EPIC deputy director John Davisson warned, “When our government compiles secret dossiers on everyday people for exercising their constitutional rights, it sends a chilling message: If you speak up, watch your back."

title: Sure, the U.S. could 'abolish ICE.' Then what? | The Seattle Times
description:

That explains why several Democratic congressional candidates are campaigning to “abolish ICE” in upcoming midterm elections.
It stokes lingering voter suspicions that Democrats don’t have a problem with ICE but with the enforcement of U.S. immigration law more broadly.
