BIDDEFORD, Maine —

The man who has been identified by family members as the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer who shot and killed a Colombian man in Biddeford last week reportedly entered protective custody just days after the shooting, according to court documents obtained by Maine's Total Coverage.

The Associated Press has reported that David Brouillette is the ICE agent who shot and killed 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero on July 13, citing accounts shared by Brouillette's first ex-wife and his 18-year-old daughter.

On Thursday, the father of Brouillette's stepdaughter filed a request for a temporary protection from abuse order against Brouillette on behalf of his daughter in Augusta District Court.

In that request, the girl's father said that Brouillette called him on the morning of July 15 and Brouillette told him that he is the ICE officer who fatally shot a man in Biddeford on July 13. According to the girl's father, Brouillette told him that his identity and home address had been posted online, so he and his wife — the girl's mother and the plaintiff's ex-wife — were leaving their home to enter government protective custody because they were receiving a large number of threats.

The court documents state that because of the events, the girl's parents agreed that she would stay with her father for the immediate future out of concern for her safety.

In his request, the girl's father also cited numerous news reports, including some from the AP, that described a long history of violence and abuse by Brouillette against his former wives and his own children.

"I am afraid that if my daughter is returned to the defendant's household or in his presence, she will be in danger — both because of the threats now directed at the defendant and anyone near him, and because of what I have since learned about his history of violence," the girl's father said in the request.

The girl's father asked the court to issue a temporary order and, after a hearing, a final order that protects his daughter by prohibiting Brouillette from having any contact with her, ordering him to stay away from her, and setting his daughter's contact with her mother's household on terms that keep her away from Brouillette.

A judge denied the request for the temporary protection from abuse order on Friday, and the girl's father chose not to proceed on his complaint for a protection order, according to the court documents.

title: UN human rights chief wins second term despite opposition from US, Israel and Russia
description:

text:
UNITED NATIONS (AP) — U.N. human rights chief Volker Türk won a second term Friday despite opposition from the United States, Russia and Israel to keep him in one of the most controversial United Nations posts for four more years.

U.N. member nations rejected a U.S. proposal to delay the vote until the end of next week as well as a Russian proposal to extend Türk’s term just until the end of the year. The vote in the 193-member General Assembly to reappoint Türk was 144-10, with 13 abstentions.

While he got strong support, the votes and speeches also reflected concern that Secretary-General António Guterres quietly nominated the Austrian lawyer this month after private consultations, with no public discussion, as the U.N. chief nears the end of his own 10-year tenure.

Türk’s job as the U.N. rights chief, by its nature, is tricky: It requires speaking out against rights violations by the governments of the countries that make up the membership of the world body. For instance, Türk has sharply criticized Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Türk got wide support but loud pushback from the U.S. and Israel

Türk, whose term was supposed to expire on Oct. 11, has faced opposition from critics and some countries for his criticism of Israel’s attacks in Gaza and his approach to China’s crackdown on its Uyghur minority. None of Türk’s predecessors have served two full terms since the job was created in 1993.

U.S. deputy ambassador Jeff Bartos warned before the vote that reappointing Türk would prove that the General Assembly “is dysfunctional” and that the vote “was quietly shoved onto the agenda at the last minute to bypass meaningful review.”

“Make no mistake, if this assembly tolerates procedural overreach, backroom deals and the misuse of U.N. posts, there will be consequences,” he warned. “The United States will immediately reassess our engagement, participation and funding.”

The Trump administration already owes nearly $4 billion to the U.N. for its regular dues and for the separate budget for U.N. peacekeeping operations.

Russia’s deputy ambassador, Dmitry Chumakov, said Guterres had sown discord among U.N. members and accused Türk of “political bias” and promoting “Western geopolitical interests under the pretext of concern for human rights.”

Speaking for the European Union, Ireland’s U.N. Ambassador Fergal Mythen reaffirmed the 27-nation bloc’s “wholehearted support” for Türk.

“The European Union believes that Mr. Türk has demonstrably fulfilled responsibilities entrusted to him effectively and with integrity in an objective and non-selective manner over the past four years,” Mythen said. He takes on another term when “the multiplication of obstacles and challenges and rights violations is relentless, and the promotion and protection of all human rights becomes ever more contested.”

Guterres, whose own second five-year term ends Dec. 31, sent letters to regional groups at the United Nations this month informing them of his intention to reappoint Türk. The African group had no objection, but the Latin American countries had several, including Nicaragua, Argentina and Paraguay.

Before the vote, Israel’s Foreign Ministry called Guterres’ action to get a second term for Türk the U.N. secretary-general’s “latest moral failure,” saying on social media that the choice should be left to his successor.

“After years of bias against Israel, the answer is accountability — not rewriting the rules,” the ministry said.

Guterres is ‘following the rules’ on the reappointment, UN says

U.N. spokesman Stephane Dujarric says Guterres was following the 1993 resolution that established a U.N. high commissioner for human rights and allows for a second term.

“The secretary-general is doing things in a very transparent manner, following the rules and his authority,” Dujarric told reporters Friday. “Consultations were had with member states prior to this and with regional groups.”

As human rights chief, the longtime U.N. functionary who worked for Guterres at United Nations headquarters in New York, Türk has expressed concerns on issues in China as diverse as the fate of detained individuals — like artist Gao Zhen, lawyer Yu Wensheng and media mogul Jimmy Lai — and counterterrorism and assimilation practices that affect ethnic minorities including the Uyghurs in the regions of Xinjiang, Inner Mongolia and Tibet.

Critics insist he could have done more to publicly follow up on a report issued by his predecessor, former Chilean President Michelle Bachelet, that said China’s discriminatory detention of Uyghurs and other mostly Muslim ethnic groups in Xinjiang may amount to crimes against humanity.

Türk also has stopped short of joining independent U.N. rights experts who have accused Israel of genocide against Palestinians during its war against Hamas in Gaza. Israel vehemently denies those claims.

Former head of Human Rights Watch Ken Roth said: “The biggest stain on Türk’s reputation is his utter abandonment of the Uyghurs.”

Türk has used both private engagement with Beijing and public advocacy to support human rights in China, his office said. Roth called that “an admission that he is doing nothing, that he’s putting the plight of the Uyghurs on the deep back burner, and is just pretending to care.”

The Chinese government denies the Uyghurs have been or are being persecuted. It maintains its policies in Xinjiang rooted out terrorism and religious extremism after sporadic bouts of violence rocked the region in previous decades.

___

Associated Press writers Jamey Keaten in Geneva, Farnoush Amiri in New York and Matthew Lee in Washington contributed to this report.

text:
Human rights initiative ByAction has clarified information regarding the possible deportation of Belarusian citizens from the United States to Belize, stressing that it has no confirmation that the relevant court orders have been carried out.

Commenting on a Reform.news report, ByAction founder Yauhen Zhdanovich said the organization has reliable information only about two decisions by the immigration court in West Los Angeles ordering the deportation of Belarusian citizens to Belize. However, human rights defenders have no confirmation that those decisions have been enforced.

“We have no confirmed information that these people were actually deported. All we know for certain is that the court ordered their deportation to Belize, but we do not know whether that decision was carried out. Most likely, it was not.

We have not been able to establish the identities of either the Belarusian citizens who were ordered deported to Belize or the attorneys who represented them. The search is ongoing. The only information we have is that the case was heard by a judge of the West Los Angeles Immigration Court,” he said.

According to Zhdanovich, it is also unknown whether an appeal was filed against the deportation order.

“We know for certain that these individuals were represented by an attorney, so it can be assumed that the decision was probably appealed. However, we have no confirmation of that,” the ByAction founder added.

ByAction has also reviewed publicly available documents concerning arrangements between the United States and Belize.

“Based on the available information, immigration authorities could face practical obstacles when attempting to enforce deportation orders that would prevent them from deporting Belarusian citizens to Belize. There are no grounds to believe that Belize was prepared to accept citizens of countries outside Latin America,” Zhdanovich said.

“At present, we are particularly concerned about the risk that our compatriots could be mistakenly deported to another country. This is the most serious challenge at the moment,” he stressed.

ByAction first published information about the immigration court decision on July 22. At the time, it said that human rights defenders were aware of two cases in which a court in California had issued such decisions.

text:
HOUSTON — A substance investigators found in a van driven by a man fatally shot by ICE earlier this month was not an illegal narcotic, the Harris County District Attorney’s Office said Friday.

Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 51-year-old father of three, was fatally shot by an ICE law enforcement officer during a July 7 traffic stop the agency said turned life-threatening. The government has alleged he weaponized the vehicle, but that argument has been disputed by others in the van.

After the fatal shooting, an FBI agent said small bags consistent with drug packaging that contained a substance resembling methamphetamine could be seen in plain view inside the vehicle. The bureau obtained a search warrant, allowing agents to search the van.

The Harris County District Attorney’s Office said Friday on X that the seized substance “tested negative for narcotics/ illicit drugs.” It said it would not comment further on the results, citing the pending investigation.

“We have notified Salgado Araujo’s family because we felt they had the right to know,” the DA’s office said.

David Donatti, senior staff attorney at the ACLU of Texas, said in a statement Friday that Salgado Araujo was a “hardworking man” who built houses for Texas families.

“The government has demonstrated that it is more interested in creating a false narrative than in seeking the truth,” he said of the search warrant. “The Salgados deserve real answers about what happened.”

Ruby L. Powers, a lawyer who represents Victor Salgado Araujo, Salgado Araujo’s brother who was taken into custody following the shooting, said previously that the substance was believed to be “granulated salt, which is paired with lemon and water as a homemade electrolyte mix used by outdoor workers in extreme Texas heat.”

Powers said Friday that full lab results expected next week will confirm what the substance was.

“An unproven claim was allowed to circulate before it was tested, and the way it was made public did real damage, diverting attention from what actually matters in this case,” she said. “Lorenzo was shot, and no lab report answers for that.”

ICE referred a request for comment on the district attorney’s finding to the Department of Homeland Security, which did not immediately respond. The FBI said it has no comment.

Caucus hearing on shooting

The finding was announced a few hours after the Congressional Hispanic Caucus held a hearing on the shooting Friday in Houston and addressed the search warrant application for the van that Salgado Araujo was driving.

Along with members of the caucus, Rep. Bennie Thompson, the ranking member on the House Homeland Security Comittee, also attended.

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said during the hearing that drug involvement would have been out of character for any of the people in the van that morning. The unsealing of the FBI’s search warrant request before a grand jury could see the investigation’s evidence was unprecedented in his career.

“To unseal it the day it’s signed, never seen it in my 20 years,” he said during the hearing.

Lawyer Hugo Balderas-Ibarra, who represents two others who were in the van, said in a statement Friday that the possibility Salgado Araujo was involved in any way with drugs is “absurd.”

Lorenzo Salgado Jr., one of Salgado Araujo’s sons, testified at the hearing, criticizing ICE and its parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security.

“Over the past two weeks we’ve had to grieve our father too soon,” he said. “DHS first said ICE targeted our father, then admitted he was never their intended target at all. DHS also said he weaponized his vehicle, a claim the three men who were in the van with him have directly disputed and one that surveillance footage, so far, does not appear to show.”

ICE personnel at the scene did not have body cameras, DHS said, and any possible security or cellphone video of the confrontation, if it exists, has not been released.

Fatal traffic stop

The government did not say narcotics activity was a reason for ICE’s traffic stop.

Salgado Araujo was driving himself and three others to a construction site for work when the confrontation took place, according to lawyers involved in the matter. His family said Salgado Araujo was in the midst of applying for legal status and had been in the country for more than three decades when he was fatally shot.

The government has not said the ICE agents suspected any controlled substances were in the vehicle or were otherwise involved when they stopped Salgado Araujo and the three others in the van. The Department of Homeland Security has not indicated that any of the people in the van had any prior criminal history or were possibly connected to controlled substances.

DHS has said that Salgado Araujo was trying to evade arrest during the traffic stop and attempted to ram ICE personnel when one fired a gun “in self-defense.”

Lawyer Balderas-Ibarra said at no point did Salgado Araujo try to harm law enforcement.

He also disputed the claim that an ICE agent was in harm’s way during the traffic stop. Homeland Security has said ICE was looking for a specific “target” when it conducted the traffic stop. U.S. Rep. Sylvia Garcia, citing her communication with ICE’s acting director, said Salgado Araujo was not that target.

The ICE officer who opened fire has not been named. The shooting remains under investigation.

DHS temporarily suspended ICE vehicle stops after the deadly shooting in Texas and another one in Maine, both of which occurred within one week, according to a senior DHS official and two former senior DHS officials. President Donald Trump swiftly overturned the decision.

Suzanne Gamboa reported from Houston and Dennis Romero from San Diego.

text:
This guide on marriage asylum case explains the interaction between marriage and asylum across UK, US, Canada, and EU. It complements our earlier marriage asylum article with fresh focus on strategic decision-making — when to pursue spouse-based route, when to maintain asylum route, and when to dual-track.[1]

Marriage during pending asylum does not automatically end the claim but opens parallel immigration options. Notification is required. Strategic analysis matters — refugee status offers benefits marriage-based status doesn't.

Legal Framework

Marriage during asylum operates under two distinct frameworks — asylum law and family/spouse immigration.[2]

Asylum claim continues — marriage doesn't automatically end.

Spouse-based route may be pursued in parallel.

Choice at grant stage — refugee status or spouse-based status.

Notification required.

UK Marriage During Asylum

Effect on Claim

Marriage doesn't end UK asylum claim. Home Office continues processing. Parallel spouse-based options open where applicable.[3]

Notification

Section 24 Immigration Act 1971 requires notification. Failure damages credibility.

Marriage to British/Settled Person

Appendix FM spouse route requires:

Minimum income £29,000 (2024; rising to £38,700 in 2025).

English language.

Genuine relationship.

Accommodation, maintenance.

Asylum seekers face challenges — no work first 12 months typically means no independent income. Spouse's income counts.

Marriage Notice (Since 2015)

Immigration Act 2014 Section 50 extended marriage notice from 28 to 70 days for persons subject to immigration control — allows investigation of suspected sham marriages.[4]

Sham Marriage Concerns

Immigration Act 1971 Section 24 criminalises sham marriages. Genuine marriages protected but scrutinised.

US Marriage During Asylum

Effect on Claim

Marriage doesn't end US asylum claim. USCIS/EOIR continues.[5]

Marriage to US Citizen/LPR

Marriage creates I-130 Petition option:

Bona fide marriage.

Petitioner status documentation.

Marriage certificate.

Genuine relationship evidence.

Marriage to USC — immediate visa availability. LPR — preference category wait.

Adjustment of Status

INA 245(a) — for applicants in US married to USC. Grounds include lawful status at entry, 245(i) grandfathering, waivers.[6]

Sham Marriage Penalties

8 USC 1325(c) — 5 years imprisonment, $250,000 fine. INA 204(c) permanent bar. Stokes interviews investigate.

Canada Marriage During Asylum

Canadian claimants who marry continue with claim. Marriage to Canadian citizen/PR creates spouse-in-Canada class under IRPR sections 130-137. Common-law and conjugal partnerships recognised.[7]

EU Marriage During Asylum

Marriage generally doesn't end asylum but opens Directive 2003/86/EC family reunification options. Sham marriage provisions apply broadly.

Strategic Considerations

Dual-Tracking

Optimal approach — pursue both routes. If asylum granted first, refugee protection with associated rights. If marriage-based succeeds first, withdraw asylum or continue (refugee status offers protections marriage doesn't).[8]

Pre-Flight Marriage

Applicants married before departure typically apply as family unit. Where family separated, family reunion post-grant is primary route.

Same-Sex Marriage

UK, Canada, US, most EU recognise same-sex marriages. LGBTQ+ asylum seekers marrying during pending claims face same framework. See our companion PSG article for LGBTQ+ analysis.

Documentation to Preserve

Marriage certificate.

Photos over time.

Joint tenancy/property.

Joint bank statements.

Communications history.

Witness statements.

Warnings

Do not enter sham marriages — severe consequences.

Notify authorities.

Seek legal advice before marriage-based route.

Consider asylum protection value.

Understand withdrawal implications.

Marriage during pending asylum doesn't end the claim. It may open alternative routes but the asylum route often provides stronger long-term protection. Dual-tracking is frequently optimal. Notification is essential.

Conclusion

text:
Two sons of a man shot by immigration officers in Houston testified at a congressional hearing Friday, describing the horror and confusion of learning their father had been killed and demanding a transparent investigation into how he died and why.

Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was killed July 7 when Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers chased his white work van through the streets, then shot him through the window in front of his work crew, including his brother.

Salgado Araujo’s sons read from prepared remarks at a Houston hearing with Democratic members of Congress. The sons' voices often choked with emotion as they described their father as a humble and hardworking family man. He lived without legal status in the U.S. for 35 years, ran a homebuilding business and had never been in trouble with the law.

“He didn’t need anybody to know his name,” Lorenzo Salgado Araujo Jr. told the hearing, held by the Congressional Hispanic Caucus. “He worked hard to protect and provide for our family, to put me and my siblings through college. He taught us that good things come to those that work hard.”

The Department of Homeland Security said shortly after the shooting that Salgado Araujo had rammed his van into the immigration vehicles chasing him, then “weaponized his vehicle in an attempt to run over an ICE law enforcement officer,” and that the officer fired in self-defense. The officers were not wearing body cameras.

Passengers in Salgado Araujo’s van describe a different version of events

At least two of the passengers in the van have disputed the government's account, saying the officers crashed into the van and were safely on the sides of the vehicle, never in danger of being struck, when the officer fired. All three passengers in the van were arrested and remain in immigration detention. One of them is Salgado Araujo’s brother, Victor, whose account of the killing is not public because his petition for release is sealed.

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare told the hearing that DHS, which oversees ICE, has ignored his requests for information and evidence, including the name of the officer who fired the fatal shot.

Nevertheless, he said, his office was making “significant progress.” He declined to discuss specific evidence or speculate on when his office’s investigation would end.

Salgado Araujo’s sons said their father would have never run from officers, who were driving unmarked vehicles, if he’d known who they were. They had talked as a family about what they would do if he encountered ICE, and they said he believed he would find a way to get back home to them.

Salgado Araujo’s sons describe an excruciating wait for information

They said he was a man of routine. The day he was killed started as most did: He woke up before dawn, his wife cooked him a hearty breakfast, then he said goodbye to her and their dog. He got into his white van, said a prayer and left before 6 a.m. to pick up his crew.

Ronaldo Salgado said his mother called him around 7 a.m. to say something bad had happened. He saw a Facebook post about an encounter with immigration officers and rushed to the scene. He was there for hours, he said, begging officers and neighbors for information, even asking one homeowner to climb onto her roof to survey the scene.

Then a Facebook video appeared.

“I learned again from a Facebook post that our dad had been shot,” he told the hearing. “Not because I could see him, but because I could hear his voice on videos posted online crying for help.”

He rushed to the hospital. More hours passed before Democratic U.S. Rep. Sylvia Garcia demanded answers, and they learned he was dead.

Garcia said the Democratic delegation has sent multiple letters to DHS and ICE about the shooting and has received no response. The delegation also invited representatives of the department and the administration to attend the hearing, and they declined.

An email sent to DHS by The Associated Press seeking comment Friday was not immediately returned.

The FBI executed a search warrant on the van, alleging that officers saw several small bags inside filled with a white substance that appeared to be methamphetamine. Salgado Araujo's sons said the insinuation that their father was involved in drug trafficking was “absurd.” The substance, the family said, was a salt mixture that the crew used as electrolytes to stay hydrated while working under the blazing sun.

Teare, the district attorney, said later Friday on the social platform X that the substance tested negative for any illegal drugs.

Lorenzo Salgado Araujo Jr. called what happened to them “a kafkaesque nightmare.” They said they mourned not only for their father but also for the families of others killed by immigration officers, including Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 26-year-old who was shot in Maine days after their father.

The sons say they want justice

The sons called on Congress to make sure justice is served.

Salgado Araujo Jr. asked people to imagine what the brothers were experiencing by picturing a loved one “pinned to the ground in pain and yelling out in desperate need of help.”

“Picture the anger and helplessness of watching that person bleed out through a video on your phone. What would you do after?” he said. “How would you cope with the feeling of losing your protector, your role model, your mother’s loving partner, your grandmother’s little boy?”

He added, “That feeling you feel right now is only a fraction of what my family and I have felt these past 17 days.”

text:
136

(OSV News) — Give those targeted in immigration enforcement operations “the chance to be heard,” said a religious sister detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents for several hours June 28, amid an intended third-country deportation effort.

On July 23, Sister Leticia Ugboaja delivered a prepared statement during a press conference hosted by Our Lady of Sorrows Church in McAllen, Texas, located at the U.S.-Mexico border.

Almost a month prior to the media event, Sister Leticia had been walking to Sunday Mass at the church, dressed in her religious habit, when ICE agents accosted and detained her. She was released after several hours following the intervention of several congressional representatives.

Accompanying Sister Leticia at the press conference were her attorney, Carlos Moctezuma García, and Sister Norma Pimentel, a member of the Missionaries of Jesus and executive director of Catholic Charities of the Rio Grande Valley, located in the Diocese of Brownsville, Texas. The diocese uploaded a recording of the full press conference to its YouTube channel.

Has worked in local healthcare for more than decade

At the press conference, Sister Leticia — a member of the Daughters of Mary Mother of Mercy, a congregation founded in Nigeria, and a registered nurse who has worked in local healthcare for more than a decade — recounted her experience in English, with Sister Norma providing a Spanish translation of the statement.

García then explained his client’s immigration status, saying that in 2019, a judge denied Sister Leticia’s petition for asylum.

Yet “in that same decision,” he said, the judge “granted her protection from removal to Nigeria” under the United Nations’ convention against torture, “finding she had met the high legal standard required to show it was more likely than not that she would face torture if returned there.”

Over the past several years, Nigeria has seen ongoing violence against both Christians and Muslims by Islamic extremists. Kidnappings of Catholic women religious were documented in 2017 and 2018, ahead of Sister Leticia’s asylum denial.

Although the judge’s removal protection “legally bars” the U.S. from deporting her to Nigeria, he said, Sister Leticia “remains as a technical matter under a final order of removal.”

‘Has done everything the law has asked of her’

However, García clarified, “she has done everything the law has asked of her,” and holds “a valid employment authorization document” while attending all required appointments with immigration officials.

He said that her June 28 detention was part of an attempt to remove Sister Leticia “not to Nigeria but to a third country,” a move that marks both “a separate legal pathway from the one her protection forecloses,” and “the subject of active litigation in federal courts nationwide.”

García said his client has a July 28 appointment with immigration officials, and expressed the hope that an ankle monitor would not be placed on Sister Leticia as part of that process.

Sister Leticia recalled that as she walked to the church, she was meditating on the Mass readings and preparing to serve as an extraordinary minister of holy Communion when agents stopped her.

“Honestly, in that moment, I did not understand what was going on, what was happening to me,” she said. “I was very much afraid, with cold sweat. I could just hear my heart, very tachycardic.”

Her long record of living and serving in the McAllen area compounded her disorientation.

‘I have walked here” countless times

“I have been in this community … more than a decade,” she said. “I have cared for the sick as a nurse in various hospitals. I did not expect (to be accosted by immigration enforcement) on an ordinary Sunday morning, when people should be ready to go to Mass, to worship the Lord, on the street here, just in front of the school. I have walked here, passed by this same road countless number of times.”

Her voice filled with emotion as she described being denied the opportunity to attend Mass.

“As we all know, Sunday Mass is obligatory,” she said. “And we have to attend Mass every day if you can. … And for me, not to go to Mass on Sunday, not to receive Communion, it was very, very heartbreaking for me.”

Sister Leticia had even implored the immigration enforcement agents for the chance to first attend the liturgy and receive holy Communion.

But “even when I told (them), ‘Can I go to Mass; can I just attend Mass, can I receive Communion?’, the answer was ‘no,'” said Sister Leticia.

‘Just a small woman’ with a rosary, key and phone

She also described feeling vulnerable as “just a small woman, a nun” with “my rosary, my key and my phone” amid “two men” who were “armed.”

The experience is “still hurting me up to today,” she said.

Saying she had “prayed a great deal” since her detention, Sister Leticia stressed that her experience was not unique.

“I am not the only one,” she said. “There are many others in this same situation — people who have been given some form of protection under our laws, who have followed every rule asked of them, and who still live with uncertainty about where they might be sent, and whether anyone will tell them before it happens.”

Sister Leticia stressed that her faith “teaches me not to be silent,” since neither silence nor fear will “solve any problem.”

Speaking out ‘of peace and honesty in my heart’

“I’m speaking this out of peace and honesty in my heart,” she said. “What I am asking is just simple. Before anyone, anyone, anyone is being taken into custody, or being taken anywhere — from home, from their parishes, from their places of work, or even walking on the streets — just … give them the chance, give them the opportunity, so that they can be heard.”

Sister Leticia added, “I believe every person in this situation like me deserves to be heard, deserves to be listened to, deserves to be given attention and opportunity, and to give them another chance to say what they have (to say).”

EAST ST. LOUIS, Ill. – United States Attorney Steven D. Weinhoeft today announced that the United States District Court for the Southern District of Illinois has ruled in favor of the United States in its lawsuit against the State of Illinois, Governor J.B. Pritzker, and multiple state entities.

The Court denied the State’s motion to dismiss and granted the United States’ cross-motion for summary judgment declaring that Illinois’ in-state tuition rules for public universities and community colleges, the RISE Act, and the Illinois DREAM Act are “unconstitutional and invalid” under the Supremacy Clause as applied to aliens not lawfully present.

“Illinois sought to incentivize illegal immigration on the taxpayer’s dime by treating illegal aliens better than U.S. citizens living in other states, in clear violation of federal law,” said U.S. Attorney Steven D. Weinhoeft. “This ruling enforces the statute Congress wrote and stops the State from putting illegal aliens ahead of American citizens.”

Federal law is clear. Under 8 U.S.C. § 1623(a), a state may not grant postsecondary education benefits to illegal aliens on the basis of residence in that state unless it makes the exact same benefit available to every United States citizen and national, without regard to where they live. Illinois chose to give preferential treatment based on residence to people here illegally. It did not extend that same treatment to American citizens who live outside Illinois. That preference is illegal.

In September 2025, the Department of Justice filed suit to stop these policies. The Court held oral argument on May 5, 2026. It has now permanently enjoined the State and the named university and college boards from enforcing the challenged provisions against aliens not lawfully present. The injunction is stayed for 14 days to permit the defendants to seek a stay pending appeal.

The case was brought by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Illinois and the U.S. Department of Justice’s Civil Division.

text:
A substance found in the work van of a Mexican immigrant killed by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent has tested negative for illicit drugs, the top prosecutor in Houston said Friday, refuting claims by federal officials that the vehicle likely contained meth.

The revelation is a major development in the case of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a construction worker who was fatally shot by an ICE officer in Houston on July 7 after living in the U.S. for 35 years. ICE has maintained Salgado Araujo "weaponized" his vehicle during an attempted traffic stop, prompting an agent to shoot him in self-defense. The other men in the van, who remain in ICE custody, have disputed that allegation.

Roughly a week or so after the killing, which was followed by another fatal shooting by an ICE agent in Maine less than a week later, the FBI submitted an affidavit in federal court saying it suspected that the van Salgado Araujo was driving contained methamphetamine. The FBI affidavit included photos taken from outside of the vehicle that showed small bags with a white crystal-like substance that an agent said was consistent with meth.

But on Friday, the office of Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare said the test results had come back negative.

"We can confirm the substance found in Lorenzo Salgado Araujo's van tested negative for narcotics / illicit drugs," the office added in a statement. "We have notified Salgado Araujo's family because we felt they had the right to know."

Teare's office said it would not be providing more details on the test results, citing an ongoing investigation.

Friday's findings are consistent with statements by representatives for the Salgado Araujo family, who had maintained the substance in question was likely granulated salt used by construction workers to create a homemade electrolyte mix to brave the summer heat.

The FBI said it did not have any comment on the test results.

In a statement Friday, David Donatti, an attorney at the ACLU of Texas, which is representing Salgado Araujo's family, said the federal government was "more interested in creating a false narrative than in seeking the truth."

"Lorenzo Salgado Araujo should still be alive today, and nothing about the government's so-called 'search' could have changed that fact," Donatti added. "That search has now proven what the Salgado family has said all along: Lorenzo was a hardworking man who made homes for Houston families."

The FBI and ICE's internal oversight office are both reviewing the July 7 shooting, though federal officials launched the investigation as one looking into the potential assault on an agent. Teare's office is conducting its own probe, and he told CBS News he's "more than prepared" to prosecute ICE agents if he finds criminal wrongdoing on their part.

ICE has said Salgado Araujo was living in the U.S. illegally, though it has not disputed that he lacked a criminal record.

In an interview with CBS News, Salgado Araujo's eldest sons, both of them American citizens, described their father as a hardworking man who loved music and his family.

"He was drawn by the promise that in America you can, if you put in the work, you'll get paid what you deserve, and the idea that in America, you can build yourself up from nothing to become someone, and to give your family a better future," Lorenzo Salgado Jr. said.

title: The Biggest Changes to Student Visas in Generations: What You Need to Know
description:
The biggest change in the rule is to limit the period of stay in the United States for international students in F status, exchange visitors in J status, and international journalists in I status.
For international journalists, that could mean living in the United States indefinitely while covering U.S. news for a paper back home.
These dates also apply to any dependents, such as children or spouses, who accompany the person to the United States.

text:
On July 17, 2026, the Trump administration unveiled the latest move in its broader efforts to reshape America’s legal immigration system. This time, it was a regulation that will lead to the greatest changes in the student visa process in 50 years, as well as changes to visas for foreign exchange visitors and for members of the international media. The new regulation is set to go into effect on September 15, unless blocked in court.

The biggest change in the rule is to limit the period of stay in the United States for international students in F status, exchange visitors in J status, and international journalists in I status. Currently, individuals granted visas in these categories can be admitted to the United States and remain for the “duration of status” — however long it takes to complete the purpose for which they got the visa. Similarly, before this rule, if USCIS approved a change of status to one of these categories for a noncitizen already in the United States, the period of stay would have been for duration of status.

For foreign students, duration of status means a person didn’t have to receive an extension from USCIS in order to finish their education, which could include graduating from their undergraduate institution and then transitioning to post-graduate optional practical training or to graduate school, or pursuing a second degree. For international journalists, that could mean living in the United States indefinitely while covering U.S. news for a paper back home. And for researchers on a J visa, that could mean staying here until their research project is complete.

What does the new rule change?

Under the new rule, these duration of status admissions are being eliminated. After September 15, 2026, foreign students and exchange visitors will be limited, based on their program length, to the end date of their specific program, or four years, whichever is shorter, plus a grace period of 30 days (down from 60 days for F-1 students under the previous rules), to depart the United States, apply for an extension if their program end date is more than four years, or pursue a different option to remain in the United States.

For international journalists, any person entering the United States after September 15, 2026, will admitted for the length of their project in the United States, or a maximum of 240 days, whichever is shorter (for journalists from China, the maximum period will be 90 days).

These dates also apply to any dependents, such as children or spouses, who accompany the person to the United States.

While people in the United States in F, J, or I status on September 15, 2026, do not have to take any action, they become subject to the deadlines, including the time limits. So, for example, an F-1 student who is in the United States on September 15, 2026, with three years left of their undergraduate program, and no eligibility for post-graduate optional practical training, would be limited to their program end date, plus the current 60-day grace period for F-1s.

If students, journalists, and exchange visitors want to stay in the country longer, then they will have to apply for an extension of status with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). International journalists will only be eligible for additional extensions limited each time to a 240 day maximum (90 days for journalists from China), while foreign students and exchange visitors will be able to extend their status to whatever the new end date for their program is or up to four years, whichever date is earlier, plus the 30-day grace period.

Importantly, extension of status requests are not free. Students, exchange visitors, or journalists seeking to stay in the United States longer will have to pay at least $420 each time they seek an extension of stay, adding to the costs of coming to the United States.

Beyond limiting the validity period of their admission, the new rule also makes significant changes to the processes for foreign students in particular. Students will now face substantially greater red tape and bureaucracy when seeking to change majors or transfer to another school.

Under the new regulation, foreign students seeking an undergraduate degree are largely banned from changing majors or transferring to another school in their first year, without exceptions that can only be granted by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in “extenuating circumstances.” DHS has made clear that the “extenuating circumstances” exception is supposed to be used only for “rare, exceptional events,” such as a natural disaster or a school shutting down.

For foreign graduate students, the rules are even more strict; they will not be permitted to change their “educational objective” at all. Graduate students’ only option if they seek to shift the purpose of their graduate program would be to transfer to another school, something that is also restricted to the case of “extenuating circumstances.”

On top of these limitations, students who graduate from a program will be banned from seeking to stay in the United States and pursue another degree, unless that degree is at a “higher educational level.” That means an undergraduate student who gets a bachelor’s degree in business could not seek to remain in the United States by enrolling in a program to seek a bachelor’s degree in math; they would only be permitted to remain if they seek to enroll in a graduate degree program.

Importantly, DHS has not yet defined exactly what the “educational levels” mean for professional degrees. For example, is a J.D. at the same, higher, or lower level than a master’s degree? Is an M.D. at the same, higher, or lower level than a Ph.D.? None of these questions are directly answered by the new rule. DHS notes in the rule that it expects to issue guidance on this point.

Crucially, DHS says that these broader restrictions on transfers and changing of degrees may be delayed up to two years if they prove difficult to implement in the short term.

The rule also makes a number of smaller changes to these visa categories which are not as consequential. For example, the rule institutes a new definition of an international media organization which may require foreign journalists to submit more paperwork in order to obtain USCIS approval. Helpfully, organizations which focus on international visas have already compiled comprehensive explainers on the new rule for impacted individuals.

What are the broader impacts of these rule changes?

Today, there are hundreds of thousands of foreign students studying at American institutions of higher education. These students are estimated to contribute roughly $43 billion a year into the U.S. economy through their tuition payments and other expenses paid while living here, and they support up to 355,000 jobs a year. However, broader efforts by the Trump administration to limit legal immigration have had a toll on the number of people interested in coming to the United States to study here. Since Trump took office, the number of international students seeking to come to the United States fell by 20 percent in total, and 24 percent at U.S. graduate programs.

The new rule does not expressly prevent any students from coming to the United States, but the additional red tape and costs may serve to drive even more students away. Most foreign students pay full tuition, helping to subsidize tuition assistance programs to American citizens. Should the number of students continue to fall, Americans may see higher tuition prices and economic struggles at colleges and universities around the country.

America’s outdated legal immigration system is already causing some of the world’s best and brightest to seek out other countries where the immigration process is not as complicated, backlogged, and expensive. While the Trump administration claims that these rules will help reduce fraud, any marginal benefit may be wiped out by the broader loss of talent that seeks out the United States.

Beyond foreign students, the changes to exchange visitors and members of the international media will again send the message that the United States is not the country it once was. Increasingly, the Trump administration is sending the message to people around the world that the United States will barely tolerate immigrants and force them to jump through as many hoops as possible to get permission to stay.

text:
(NewsNation) — Federal prosecutors Friday detailed a deadly human trafficking ring in which immigrants were transported illegally in Union Pacific railroad car shipping containers, which eventually led to the May deaths of seven people from Mexico and Honduras who were left gasping for air before they died in the sweltering Texas heat.

Nine of 11 people targeted by federal prosecutors are in custody, Justice Department officials announced, months after the bodies of six immigrants were discovered inside a railcar in Laredo, Texas. The body of a seventh man was found near train tracks in San Antonio. NewsNation previously reported that the deaths were linked to a larger human smuggling operation.

Investigators previously announced that the death of the man found along the tracks was also tied to the same smuggling operation.

The 11 defendants, including Karina Garcia, face charges of conspiracy to transport illegal immigrants that resulted in death and aiding and abetting the transportation of illegal immigrants resulting in death, court documents show.

Four of those indicted are U.S. citizens, two lawful U.S. permanent residents and five migrants in the U.S. illegally, federal prosecutors said. Garcia and another co-defendant, Seferino Huerta-Casillas, remain at large, prosecutors announced Friday, adding that they are currently unaware of their location. Those indicted Friday face life in prison if convicted.

Prosecutors said that the victims participated in a human smuggling organization that illegally used the train system to smuggle migrants further into the United States after illegally crossing them from Mexico. The ring began operating in April 2023 and continued through May of this year, when the bodies were discovered inside the storage container in Laredo.

“It’s May, and it’s Texas and ultimately, very hard to survive in an un-air-conditioned, sealed container with … the temperature being what it was on that day,” U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Texas Justin Simmons said at a news conference Friday.

How the human smuggling ring operated

The indictment indicates that each migrant paid what equated to between $ 1,500 and $10,000 to individuals in Honduras, Mexico, the United States and elsewhere to be transported illegally into the interior of the United States.

Once smuggled into the United States, immigrants were often housed in stash houses or in the brush along the Union Pacific tracks in Del Rio, which sits on the banks of the Rio Grande River. Members of the smuggling organization would load immigrants into shipping containers, which allowed those who had been smuggled into the country to travel deeper into the U.S. without detection, court documents show.

The smuggling operation involved multiple smugglers, who worked together, federal prosecutors said, to accomplish their goals. This included the coordination of routes, smuggling guides, stash house operators and drivers.

Authorities identified the victims as migrants from Honduras and Mexico, including a 14-year-old boy. The medical examiner determined at least one victim died from heat stroke, and that was likely the cause of death for the others as they were trapped inside the shipping container.

Federal prosecutors said that on the day that the seven victims were loaded into the shipping containers, the temperature hovered between 88 and 92 degrees. But the medical examiner said the temperatures inside the containers were much higher, likely between 120 and 150 degrees.

Investigators previously reported that the Union Pacific train left Long Beach, California, on Thursday, May 7, and arrived in Laredo on May 10. The bodies were discovered by a Union Pacific employee at around 3:30 p.m. local time, and the Webb County Medical Examiner determined that the six people likely died before arriving in Laredo.

The indictment released Friday said that as the temperatures inside the storage containers rose, the immigrants trapped inside panicked. One of the immigrants sent a text message to an out-of-state relative, pleading for help while the others began sweating profusely and gasping for air.

Simmons said that the likely destination of the immigrants was San Antonio, but they continued onto Laredo after smugglers opened the container to find the smuggled passengers “in peril.” Smugglers fled the scene, leaving the six immigrants to die inside the container and a seventh along the railroad tracks, where his body was found by local police the next day after it fell from the train.

A Union Pacific employee working at the rail yard in Laredo, Texas, discovered the bodies when the worker noticed a leg sticking out from one of the containers. That led to the discovery of the rest of the victims, who medical officials said were likely dead by the time they arrived in Laredo.

Friday’s indictments were announced months after Mayra Huerta of Del Rio, Texas, was charged with harboring migrants in the U.S. illegally, according to a federal complaint filed after the deaths, which identified Huerta as a known facilitator of the larger human smuggling ring.

Huerta was arrested after investigators found $53,000 in cash at a house she said she shared with her husband and his nephew. Investigators also seized multiple weapons at the home, where Huerta was found. Her husband and his nephew escaped into Mexico by crossing the river, sources previously told NewsNation.

Sources also indicated Huerta was paid for stashing immigrants at her home and passed the money along to the smuggling operation’s two main facilitators.

A previous smuggling operation led to the discovery of 53 bodies inside a tractor-trailer in Laredo in 2023. In that case, Simmons said those found inside the semi-truck paid between $10,000 and $15,000 to be smuggled into the United States.

“The message today is this: Those thinking about entering this country illegally, don’t,” Simmons said. “There is a legal pathway for you to come into this country. You do not have to hand your life over to smugglers and the cartels with which they work. They don’t care about your life. They only care about your money.”

text:
Up until this week, House representative and Democratic Senate candidate Haley Stevens’s campaign shared a mutual consultant with far right tech surveillance company Palantir, new reporting reveals, bringing renewed attention to Stevens’s record on ICE as she faces a contentious race against Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan.

Drop Site News’s Ryan Grim reported on Thursday that the consultant, Caitlin Legacki, was consulting for Stevens’s communications outfit while also “secretly” consulting for Palantir. Legacki was “one of Stevens’ key spokespeople,” as local outlet Michigan Advance wrote.

After Grim reached out to the campaign for comment on Legacki’s dual appointment, they terminated her and said that Stevens was “unaware” of her work for the tech giant. Legacki is also a senior fellow at conservative Democrat-aligned think tank Third Way, Grim reports.

The campaign also replied with a statement touting Stevens’s record on Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Palantir has been central to ICE and the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) mass deportation efforts. Among other collaborations, ICE granted Palantir a $30 million contract last year to build out a surveillance program to track the movements of immigrants.

“Haley believes ICE is out of control, putting Michiganders in danger, and needs an immediate overhaul. That’s why she’s voted against giving them another cent without serious reforms, including prosecuting any ICE agents who commit crimes and abuse their power, forcing ICE agents to wear proper ID and prohibiting them from wearing masks to conceal their identities, and taking away their $75 billion slush fund,” the campaign said.

However, Stevens has previously come under fire for her record on ICE. In February, Stevens visited a Michigan ICE jail where an immigrant who was being detained, Nenko Gantchev, died. After the visit, she praised the facility for employing women — a comment that was mocked online.

“Of note, there is female leadership here, and there are women who walked with us today and explained, on the intake process, how important it is to treat people with humanity,” Stevens said, Michigan Advance reported at the time. “And that obviously really stuck out to me, because some of the things that we are witnessing before our eyes, in our neighborhoods, in our streets, is really a lack of humanity.”

Stevens has also been criticized for being one of 75 Democrats who voted for a resolution that expresses “gratitude to law enforcement officers, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement personnel,” after an attack at a mall in Boulder, Colorado last year.

“Congresswoman Stevens said she’ll stand up to ICE, all while she took talking points and advice from a compromised corporate apologist now revealed to be a key advisor in Trump’s deportation machine,” said a spokesperson for El-Sayed’s campaign, Roxie Richner, in a statement. “Perhaps it’s why Stevens voted to thank and fund ICE. Abdul has been clear and consistent on his stance since 2018: Abolish ICE.”

Stevens — who was first elected to Congress by primarying incumbent Rep. Andy Levin with the help of AIPAC, in 2022 — is locked in a fierce race against former public health official and progressive candidate El-Sayed.

title: Beyond the Border: Detained witnesses, diverted FEMA staff and ICE's record arrest number
description:
The Charlotte Observer reported that ICE detained a Somali immigrant who had been living in the U.S. for decades and deported him to Somalia.
A 78-year-old Ugandan pastor in ICE custody told The Washington Post that he has lost 35 pounds and can no longer walk.
The Denver Post reported that the family of a Colorado man who died in ICE custody last year is still seeking answers.
KCUR reported that ICE detained an Ecuadorian asylum seeker after agents raided a market in Kansas City using a warrant with no named individuals.
The Chicago Tribune reported that ICE detained a school custodian at an asylum check-in and sent him to a jail in Indiana, separating him from his family.
text:
Here's what happened this week in immigration news.

Written by Rami Alarian, Edited by Kate Morrissey

Welcome to another edition of Beyond the Border, which summarizes immigration news from across the country in a weekly roundup. Did we miss something? Message us via kate@daylightsandiego.org or on Instagram.

Want to support this work? Consider donating to Daylight San Diego or email lauren@daylightsandiego.org if you're interested in sponsoring this newsletter.

Mistreatment in Custody

The Guardian reported that a Wisconsin mosque president said he lost over 30 pounds over 80 days in ICE custody and endured treatment similar to Israeli prison.

The Charlotte Observer reported that ICE detained a Somali immigrant who had been living in the U.S. for decades and deported him to Somalia. His niece said he suffered injuries during transport.

A man with a disability is suing ICE along with private prison companies GeoGroup and CoreCivic, alleging agents beat him unconscious during his arrest and that detention center staff mocked his disability, telling him he’d never walk again, Mother Jones reported.

A 78-year-old Ugandan pastor in ICE custody told The Washington Post that he has lost 35 pounds and can no longer walk. His parishioners, many of them Trump supporters, feel conflicted about what's happening to him.

The New Yorker took a deep dive into the creation of Camp East Montana, a notorious tent detention complex on a West Texas military base holding thousands of people in ICE custody. A former ICE official said the administration’s goal is “to make detention look and feel so bad that people leave.”

The Washington Post reported that a Human Rights Watch and American Civil Liberties Union report found that 90% of detainees interviewed at Camp East Montana in Texas reported being beaten or witnessing beatings. Detainees also reported denied medical care, feces-covered bathrooms and spoiled food.

The Denver Post reported that the family of a Colorado man who died in ICE custody last year is still seeking answers. The man had agreed to voluntary departure to Nicaragua, but ICE had still kept him in custody. ICE said his death was a suicide.

The Washington Post reported that United States immigration officials alerted others about dangerous overcrowding for weeks in New York’s 26 Federal Plaza immigration facility, but the agency kept adding more people.

Increased arrests

The Guardian reported that ICE arrested over 43,000 people in June, a record number since President Donald Trump returned to office. The agency has shifted to less visible arrests at workplaces, homes and check-in appointments.

The Washington Post reported that ICE averaged more than 1,400 arrests daily in the first 12 days of July, setting the highest pace of Trump’s second term.

ICE agents entered Manolo Farmers Market in El Cajon, California, on Sunday, but they left soon after employees and customers demanded to see a warrant, El Imparcial reported.

KCUR reported that ICE detained an Ecuadorian asylum seeker after agents raided a market in Kansas City using a warrant with no named individuals. The wife of the asylum seeker found out about her husband’s arrest through videos on social media.

Houston Public Media reported that ICE released an 18-year-old Russian immigrant on Monday after detaining him three days earlier at Houston Hobby Airport.

The Chicago Tribune reported that ICE detained a school custodian at an asylum check-in and sent him to a jail in Indiana, separating him from his family.

ICE-related deaths

More than 100 people attended a Houston city hall meeting to demand an independent investigation into an ICE officer's killing of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, The Guardian reported.

The Houston Chronicle reported that three men detained at the scene dispute the government's claim that Salgado Araujo rammed an agent’s vehicle.

La Jornada reported that Salgado Araujo’s brother, who witnessed the killing, remains detained at an ICE facility in Conroe, Texas.

Mother Jones compiled a list of lies that ICE and the Department of Homeland Security have told after using force in ways that injured or killed people.

The Miami Herald identified the man killed by a truck while fleeing ICE officials as a 28-year-old Mexican father and tourist on a valid visa.

The Associated Press identified the ICE Officer who shot Joan Durán Guerrero in Maine last week as David Brouillette, and the outlet found that he had a history of domestic violence.

Brouillette's ex-wife told NPR that Brouillette has a violent past and racist beliefs.

CNN reported that Brouillette said that he suffered lingering cognitive issues after a head injury in 2021.

Other News

Immigration judges nationwide are denying bond more often, with the sharpest jump at California’s Adelanto detention facility, the LAist reported. A group of immigration attorneys has sued for public records related to the change.

ICE has issued a new dress code that bans field officers from wearing jeans, hoodies and graphic tees, requiring visible badges and ballistic vests instead, The Intercept reported.

The Arizona Republic reported that a House Democrats report found the Department of Homeland Security illegally diverted FEMA staff to serve as the “operational backbone” of ICE’s mass deportation efforts.

The Intercept reported that Google has deleted nearly all Google Maps reviews of ICE detention facilities.

A Phoenix jury delivered a not-guilty verdict for a man charged with assaulting a federal officer after he ran over to help his father, whom the man said was being pummeled by immigration officials, The Arizona Republic reported.

ABC7 reported that the Los Angeles Police Department is letting a three-year contract with Flock Safety expire over civil liberties and data privacy concerns. The department is continuing talks with Flock about a revised contract.

Citizens Bank is cutting ties with CoreCivic and GEO Group after a campaign led by advocacy groups and city councils threatened to pull funds, Associated Press reported.

Thanks for reading! Take care and stay well.

— Rami

title: New Legislation Targets Birthright Citizenship in Territories Like Puerto Rico | Truthout
authors: britney, Amy Goodman, Juan González, Justin Akers Chacón, Chris Walker, Sharon Zhang, Evan Vorpahl, Chip Gibbons, David Armiak, Freddy Brewster
description:

But first, Professor Efrén Rivera Ramos, if you can talk about this effort to strip citizenship, or birthright citizenship, for some in Puerto Rico?

text:
After failing to overturn birthright citizenship at the Supreme Court, Republican legislators are turning to new tactics to disenfranchise people born on U.S. soil. Their latest targets are those born to noncitizen or permanent resident parents in U.S. territories like Puerto Rico, where the Supreme Court has said citizenship is granted by statute and full constitutional protections do not apply. The proposed “End Birthright Citizenship for the Territories Act” would create “a subclass of people who can be discriminated against” and “disregarded as human beings” in the U.S. territories, says Puerto Rican legal scholar Efrén Rivera Ramos, who joins Democracy Now! from Puerto Rico’s capital city, San Juan. While the bill’s sponsor, Republican Congressmember Morgan Griffith of Virginia, says he’s focused only on so-called birth tourism, Rivera Ramos says the language of the law is less clear.

The quasi-colonial status of Puerto Rico is also being highlighted by the 10th anniversary of PROMESA, the Obama-era legislation that created a U.S.-appointed fiscal control board to manage the island’s finances and restructure debt. In practice, PROMESA “has been a failure,” says Rivera Ramos, asserting the anti-democratic structure has imposed austerity measures and done little to address corruption, waste and inefficiency that plague the economy.

TRANSCRIPT

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan González.

Last week, Virginia Republican Congressmember Morgan Griffith introduced the End Birthright Citizenship for the Territories Act, which would limit automatic citizenship in Puerto Rico and other U.S. territories to only children born to U.S. citizens or legal permanent residents starting in 2027. Congressman Griffith said in a press release his focus is on cracking down on, quote-unquote, “birth tourism,” and that while the Supreme Court affirmed last month that birthright citizenship is a constitutional right, it also, quote, “leaves the door open,” unquote, for congressional action on citizenship in the U.S. territories.

His legal reasoning relies on the controversial early-20th-century cases known as the Insular Cases, in which the Supreme Court ruled the Constitution doesn’t fully apply to the territories, saying the, quote-unquote, “uncivilized” races who, quote-unquote, “infest” the territories are, quote-unquote, “unfit.”

In a press release, Griffith said, quote, “Just like Congress possesses the power to grant the territories Constitutional rights in statute, we have the power to take them away in statute.” The legislation would impact Guam, Puerto Rico, the Northern Mariana Islands and the U.S. Virgin Islands. People born in American Samoa are already not classified as citizens. Vice President JD Vance has said on Fox News he’s in favor of the idea.

This latest attempt to restrict rights in the U.S. territories coincides with the 10th anniversary of PROMESA, the law that established a fiscal control board in Puerto Rico to oversee finances on the island and restructure its debt, but its power and impact extends far beyond that. The law was passed in June 2016.

For more, we turn now to two guests. Efrén Rivera Ramos joins us from San Juan. He’s a law professor, former dean at the University of Puerto Rico Law School and author of The Legal Construction of Identity: The Judicial and Social Legacy of American Colonialism in Puerto Rico. And we’re joined by Juan Carlos Dávila. He’s here with us in our New York studio, filmmaker, activist and journalist from Puerto Rico. His latest film for PBS is titled Farmers of the Sea, the third in a trilogy of films on the Puerto Rican working class. And we’re going to talk about that documentary in a minute.

But first, Professor Efrén Rivera Ramos, if you can talk about this effort to strip citizenship, or birthright citizenship, for some in Puerto Rico? Explain what’s going on here.

EFRÉN RIVERA RAMOS: Well, thank you very much.

What I would like to say is that this is obviously an attempt to start tampering with the citizenship situation of the people of the territories. The title of the bill that has been presented is to end birthright citizenship in the territories. Now, that’s a very broad concept, and it could lead to other developments in the future that would affect — could affect the citizenship status of everybody in Puerto Rico, or everybody born in Puerto Rico or in the other territories. So, I would like to raise a flag about that possibility.

The bill itself, if read generously, says that if the bill is passed, as of January 1st, 2027, children born of non-U.S. citizens and non-U.S. residents living in Puerto Rico would not be considered U.S. citizens anymore, as it is now. Now anybody born in Puerto Rico, regardless of the citizenship status of her parents, is considered a U.S. citizen. And that has been so since a combination of statutes passed by Congress starting 1917 and ending in 1941.

The congressperson, Griffith, said in a statement that this would impact only the children of those who are living in Puerto Rico without being permanent residents or U.S. citizens. Now, if you read the bill, that is not what it says in the first part of the bill. That, if you read just the first part of the bill, it says that people born in Puerto Rico from 1941 to 2027 would be considered U.S. citizens, but not after that. It is not until the very last provision of the bill that it tries to clarify that this applies only to children born of non-U.S. citizens and non-U.S. residents. So, there is a degree of ambiguity in the way that the bill is constructed that may cause problems in the future.

But even if it is interpreted the way that the congressman has said, it does create problems for substantial sectors of people living in Puerto Rico. We do have a substantial immigrant population. Most of it comes from the Dominican Republic, although we also have immigrants from Haiti and from other parts of Latin America and the Caribbean. If the bill is passed, the effect would be to create a very special underclass of people living in Puerto Rico who will lose many of its rights, many of the rights that they may enjoy right now. This would be like creating a minority within a minority, in the sense that after the U.S. Supreme Court case Barbara v. Trump, children born of nonresidents and non-U.S. born in the United States, people born in the United States under those circumstances are still considered citizens. If the bill is passed, an exception will be made for those born under the same conditions in Puerto Rico and the territories. So, this is an attempt at creating a subclass of people who can be discriminated against even more and who could be — who could be simply disregarded as human beings with rights living within the jurisdiction of the United States, because the territories, after all, are placed under the jurisdiction of the United States. So, that would be my concern.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: Professor Rivera Ramos, I wanted to ask you also about the PROMESA situation. It’s 10 years since Congress and President Obama set up PROMESA. It was supposed to be a temporary fiscal control board. And yet here we are, 10 years later, and it is still effectively running the affairs of the island of Puerto Rico, a U.S.-appointed board, effectively ending the claims of the United States that Puerto Rico was an autonomous territory. I’m wondering your sense of where PROMESA goes from here. Have the people of Puerto Rico become accustomed to having their decisions made by an appointed group of largely outsiders?

EFRÉN RIVERA RAMOS: Well, I think that many people have become accustomed to that, although we can also witness, have witnessed, a growing criticism of the board. It is viewed by many people in Puerto Rico, with reason, as a colonial entity that was imposed by the U.S. Congress upon Puerto Rico and Puerto Ricans. As you have said, it is an unelected board that exercises a great deal of power over Puerto Rico. It has taken over many of the governmental operations of the Puerto Rican government, I mean. And it has made decisions that have had a very deleterious effect on Puerto Rico and on many sectors of Puerto Rico, especially the most vulnerable.

The board has focused its operations on the fiscal end of the economy of Puerto Rico. And I think it is the consensus of most economists in Puerto Rico that that has been a huge mistake. Puerto Rico is in need of an economic development plan, of strengthening the provision of essential services to the population, of having a sound economic policy in place, of getting rid of many distortions of the economy, such as corruption, waste, incompetence, etc. And the board has done almost nothing regarding those very crucial aspects of the Puerto Rican economy.

So, I think that some people might say that the board has had some positive effect in terms of the restructuring of the debt, but even that hasn’t been as important as it was needed to be done, and it has entirely disregarded the economic development aspects of the Puerto Rican economy. So, I think that in the end, it has been a failure.

text:
Family and friends of a Jamaican-born flight attendant are asking for him to be released from ICE detention.

On a GoFundMe set up to help Lorenzo Thompson pay his legal fees and other expenses, his best friend, Kristin Foster, said: "He came to the United States legally from Jamaica in 2021 seeking safety from life-threatening abuse."

Thompson is a flight attendant with Southwest and was detained by ICE officers on July 14, according to his friends and confirmed by ICE.

"So this one was a tough one for me because again, he is a ray of sunshine. So, It's very difficult to see him in this situation," said Tremaine Hemans, Thompson's attorney.

The Department of Homeland Security told FOX 17 News Thompson overstayed his visa by nearly five years.

MORE NEWS | 3 Cuban nationals arrested in Tennessee human trafficking bust

The agency said Thompson entered the United States on a visa on April 17, 2021. The visa expired Oct. 16, 2021.

"He has a valid application that was filed in the amount of time he was supposed to file it you know, and you are taking years to make a decision on this, so you can't turn around and blame the person for your inefficiency," said Hemans.

Hemans did not provide specifics as to what that application was or what kind of visa he had, but claimed he had work authorization.

A federal source told FOX 17 News Thompson has pending asylum and no previous criminal history.

But what does federal law say about this case?

Doug Russo, owner of Rose Immigration Law firm, said overstaying a visa is a civil violation-not criminal, but it doesn't stop someone from being detained.

"It's certainly a civil offense when someone overstays their visa, and at the same time that does put somebody at risk for being detained," he said.

He argues pending asylum cases take too long, leaving people like Thompson in limbo.

"One of the unique features of asylum law is that an individual may have a pending asylum claim while simultaneously lacking a separate underlying immigration status," said Thompson.

Hemans believes this case highlights who ICE is detaining.

"He also is the face for many people who are dealing with this same scenario," said Hemans.

Russo said ultimately an immigration judge makes the decision on whether or not Thompson is deported.

ICE also said Thompson "will remain in ICE custody pending his immigration proceedings."

Thompson is currently in ICE custody in Natchez, Mississippi.

TWU Local 556 posted on Instagram that it stands by its members.

Foster also sent us this statement in part:

"We are incredibly grateful for the outpouring of love, prayers, encouragement, and generosity that has been shown to Lorenzo and our family during this difficult time. Your support has meant more than words can express, and it has reminded us that we are not walking this journey alone.

At this time, we respectfully ask for your understanding as we are unable to publicly discuss the details of Lorenzo’s legal case or answer questions regarding ongoing proceedings. Out of respect for the legal process, and to ensure that nothing said publicly could unintentionally impact or jeopardize his case, we have been advised to keep specific matters private.

Our focus right now is supporting Lorenzo, working closely with his legal team, and remaining hopeful for a positive outcome. We kindly ask for your continued prayers, patience, and support as we navigate the road ahead.

Thank you to everyone who has donated, shared his story, reached out with kind words, and stood beside us during this time. Your compassion and unwavering support have been a source of strength for Lorenzo and everyone who loves him. We will share updates when we are able to do so. His attorney will make a statement.

With sincere gratitude,

Lorenzo’s Family & Friends"

Southwest Airlines did not respond to FOX 17 News for comment.

text:
WASHINGTON—From Hot Springs, Ark. to Houston, from a church on Grant Circle in D.C., to sites in Washington state, MoveOn.org and its allies plan to protest on July 25 against the latest killings—two in one week—by President Trump’s ICE agents.

But the outrage over ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) agents’ killing of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston and Johan Sebastian Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine, apparently hasn’t moved the Trump regime or its congressional Republican sycophants.

Trump Homeland Security Department Secretary Mark Wayne Mullin floated the idea of reining in ICE, which is part of his department, by ordering its agents to cease their extensive traffic stops. Trump promptly overruled Mullin, via a late-night tweet on his Truth Social platform.

And before that, Congress’s ruling Republicans enacted, and Trump signed, a law doling out billions of dollars to fund ICE through the rest of Trump’s presidential term and beyond, into fiscal 2029.

Which won’t stop MoveOn and its allies, especially since the organization reports, witnesses to Salgado’s murder have been detained by ICE and held in its concentration camps, while Guerrero was shot down as his spouse and three-year-old daughter looked on, traumatized.

authors: Sophie Hurwitz, Daniella Jiménez, Renée Bartlett-Webber, Ellie Prickett-Morgan, Samantha Michaels, Noah Lanard, Erin Siegal McIntyre, Anna Merlan, Molly Taft, Nitish Pahwa
description:
Brouillette is no outlier, said Lynn Tramonte, Executive Director of the Ohio Immigrant Alliance and author of the report.
This is not the first report alleging systemic sexual abuse by ICE and Border Patrol agents.
Here at Mother Jones, journalist Erin Siegal McIntyre investigated one alleged rape at the Border Patrol Academy in 2024.
The federal immigration policing force now includes about 50,000 agents spanning ICE, CBP, and other law enforcement agencies.
